The positive economic performance was accompanied by substantial capital inflows, which led to significant appreciation in financial asset prices in 2017 and early 2018 (Chart 2.10, blue and pink bars). Capital inflows into regional markets rebounded significantly in 2017, with total portfolio investment inflows reaching their highest level since 2010. Valuations of various financial assets in the region also rose with the market rally. Indeed, credit risk spreads in the region narrowed further in the second half of 2017, while benchmark equity indices across the region rose broadly. Regional currencies generally appreciated against the US dollar.

Backed by buoyant domestic demand and improved export performance, Hong Kong's economy maintained solid growth drivers in the second half of 2017. Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. The economic outlook for Hong Kong continues to be subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including monetary policy normalisation by major central banks, stability of global financial markets, rising protectionist sentiments, and escalating geopolitical tensions. In the near term, while domestic inflationary pressures should remain moderate, certain upside risks persist.  Hong Kong's economy sustained its growth drivers in the second half of 2017. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew by 0.8% quarter-on-quarter in both the third and fourth quarters, broadly similar to the average growth of 0.9% in the preceding two quarters (Chart 3.1). Compared with the first half of the year, private consumption continued to grow solidly and remained one of the key drivers of GDP growth. The robust growth in consumption was underpinned by favourable employment and income conditions, continued optimism in consumer sentiment, and positive wealth effects from rising asset prices. Although building and construction activities moderated, increased business capital spending led aggregate investment spending to rise notably in the final quarter after three quarters of broadly stable performance. On the external front, benefiting from improved global trade growth and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism, Hong Kong's export performance improved further (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as imports grew faster than exports, net exports of goods continued to drag on GDP growth, while net exports of services contributed positively to GDP growth.  Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports  Sustained economic growth drove an increase in jobs in the second half of 2017. Total employment rose by around 0.7% to over 3.85 million during the period, with the most notable increases in the construction sector, the finance and business services sector, and the public administration, social and personal services sector. As real GDP growth outpaced employment growth, there were signs of further improvement in labour productivity.  Economic growth is expected to remain robust in 2018. On the external front, Hong Kong's export performance will continue to benefit from an improved global economic growth outlook and the gradual recovery of inbound tourism. On the domestic front, private consumption is expected to continue growing, mainly driven by favourable labour market conditions. In light of the eventual rise in HKD interest rates, Feature 3 examines the impact of higher mortgage burden on private consumption. As for domestic fixed capital formation, building and construction activities should grow steadily, supported by increased housing supply and ongoing infrastructure projects. While an improved economic environment will stimulate business capital spending, a possible upward adjustment in interest rates may exert adverse effects. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3% and 4% for 2018, while international and private sector analysts project growth of between 2% and 4%. Nevertheless, Hong Kong's growth prospects remain subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the external environment mentioned in earlier chapters, the economic performance of Mainland China amid tightening financial conditions, and developments in Hong Kong's asset markets.  Domestic inflationary pressures remained contained in the second half of 2017, though month-on-month inflation momentum showed signs of a slight pick-up in recent months. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 1.7% and 1.6% in the third and fourth quarters respectively, broadly in line with the average increase of around 1.7% in the first half of the year. However, the 3-month annualised rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, edged up to 2.8% in January 2018 (Chart 3.3). Both traded goods and services prices rose. The recovery of fresh-letting private residential rentals since mid-2016 may also have contributed to some extent to increased inflation momentum (Chart 3.4). Meanwhile, labour cost pressures remained moderate in recent quarters (Chart 3.5).  Chart 3.3 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Chart 3.4 CPI rental component and market rentals Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and per capita wages  With global inflation remaining subdued and domestic costs rising at a stable pace, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are expected to stay moderate in 2018, though the underlying inflation rate may gradually pick up from its eight-year low of 1.7% in 2017. For instance, inflationary pressures could intensify in the second half of 2018 as a result of the pass-through effects from increases in fresh-letting private residential rentals. Market consensus forecasts put headline inflation at a moderate 2.2% in 2018, while the Government's forecast for underlying inflation is 2.5%. Despite the benign inflation outlook, upside risks remain. On the external front, any unexpected surge in global inflation or commodity prices could add to domestic inflation momentum. On the domestic front, the labour market has tightened further recently, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling from 3.4% in 2016 to 2.9% in December 2017, dropping below 3% for the first time in nearly 20 years (Chart 3.6). With the output gap estimated to be close to zero, a significant tightening of the labour market could exert additional upward pressure on inflation.  Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate  Following the period of low interest rates after the 2008 global financial crisis, mortgage indebtedness among Hong Kong households has increased. As the normalisation of USD counterparts progresses, HKD interest rates will eventually follow suit and rise, leading to a corresponding increase in households' mortgage burden in the future, which will in turn weigh on household consumption. This feature therefore examines the impact of an increase in mortgage burden on private consumption in Hong Kong.  Mortgage burden refers to the ratio of mortgage debt servicing payments (i.e. interest payments plus principal repayments) to income. Chart B3.1 illustrates the role of mortgage burden in the transmission of interest rate shocks to private consumption. In addition to the substitution effect, income effect, wealth effect, and collateral effect from asset price changes as discussed in standard economic theory, in the presence of a mortgage burden, interest rate shocks can also affect private consumption by altering mortgage interest payments, which in turn change households' disposable income. This effect will be amplified as outstanding mortgage debt increases. Furthermore, principal repayments will vary with changes in outstanding mortgage debt, which will also affect private consumption through changes in households' disposable income.  Chart B3.1 Determinants of private consumption  To measure the impact of mortgage burden on private consumption, we estimate the outstanding mortgage debt servicing ratio (OMDSR) based on outstanding mortgage liabilities. Unlike existing mortgage burden indicators that only apply to newly extended mortgage liabilities, the OMDSR covers total outstanding household mortgage liabilities, which are more closely associated with aggregate private consumption. Following broadly the methodology used by the Bank for International Settlements, we measure the OMDSR using the standard formula for fixed annuity payments:  where Dt denotes outstanding residential mortgage loan balances in the banking sector, Yt represents the total income of owner-occupier households (proxied by the median income of owner-occupier households multiplied by the number of owner-occupier households), and rt and st denote the average interest rate and maturity of outstanding mortgage loans respectively.  To assess whether the OMDSR can reliably measure the mortgage burden of the household sector as a whole, it is useful to compare the OMDSR with two commonly used debt servicing burden indicators. Chart B3.2 presents the estimated OMDSR from 1985 to mid-2017, together with the median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income estimated by the Census and Statistics Department based on quinquennial population censuses. Both ratios exhibited a declining trend in the early 2000s, consistent with the reduction in overall household mortgage borrowing and the substantial fall in mortgage rates following the burst of the housing market bubble in 1997. Despite the sharp rise in property prices after the global financial crisis, both ratios remained stable, owing to the HKMA's macro-prudential measures on bank mortgage lending, which curbed overall household mortgage leverage. In addition, the extension of new mortgage loan tenors also reduced the actual amount of mortgage payments.  Chart B3.2 OMDSR and median ratio of mortgage payments and loan repayments to income  We also compare the OMDSR with banks' debt servicing ratio, which is the actual debt servicing-to-income ratio of new mortgage applicants at banks. As shown in Chart B3.3, the OMDSR is lower than banks' debt servicing ratio, partly because the OMDSR covers not only new mortgages but also existing mortgages. Since existing mortgages were originated when housing prices were lower, their debt servicing payments are correspondingly lower than those of new mortgages. Therefore, the outstanding mortgage burden indicator covering both existing and new mortgages (i.e. the OMDSR) is lower than the debt servicing burden indicator for new mortgages (i.e. banks' debt servicing ratio). Furthermore, banks' debt servicing ratio is also higher because banks, in compliance with the HKMA's prudential regulatory requirements, include non-mortgage loan repayments when calculating the debt servicing ratio. Following the global financial crisis, both the OMDSR and banks' debt servicing ratio have remained stable, primarily due to the HKMA's implementation of prudential supervision of mortgage lending, which sets an upper limit on banks' debt servicing ratio, a measure that has also helped to stabilise the OMDSR.  Chart B3.3 OMDSR and banks' debt servicing ratio for new mortgages  Overall, the OMDSR is broadly consistent with commonly used debt servicing burden indicators, but possesses greater timeliness and is able to reflect the burden of total outstanding mortgage liabilities rather than just new mortgage liabilities. We therefore believe that using the OMDSR can help assess the impact of mortgage burden on private consumption.  To evaluate the impact of mortgage burden on private consumption in Hong Kong, we estimate an error-correction model following the approaches of Lai and Lam (2002) and Kang (2016). In this model, the long-run relationship between real private consumption (proxied by real per-household private consumption) and its determinants is captured by an error-correction term in the short-run specification. Based on established theoretical and empirical evidence, we incorporate real income (proxied by median household income deflated by the composite consumer price index), real housing and financial wealth (proxied by residential property prices and the Hang Seng Index respectively, deflated by the composite consumer price index), and the OMDSR as the long-run determinants of private consumption.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened, while the local interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. Total lending continued to increase in the second half of 2017, but the pace of growth moderated compared with the first half. Looking ahead, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure as US monetary policy continues to normalise. If global financial market sentiment shifts abruptly, volatility in capital flows may increase. In the second half of 2017, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate moved between 7.799 and 7.827 (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate strengthened briefly and stayed close to 7.80 during September to November 2017. This was mainly due to tighter liquidity conditions driven by increased funding demand from IPO activities and banks' prudent approach to manage their liquidity ahead of month-end and year-end, which in turn slowed interest rate arbitrage activities and increased short-covering of Hong Kong dollar short positions. As the tightening of Hong Kong dollar liquidity eased and US dollar commercial demand rose towards year-end, the Hong Kong dollar spot exchange rate softened again in mid-December 2017. Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar continued to operate in an orderly manner despite increased volatility in global financial markets, particularly equity markets. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakened against the US dollar, but the CUs were not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Capital Flow Indicators The nominal effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar fluctuated mildly in the second half of 2017, but recently faced greater downward pressures as the US dollar weakened further (Chart 4.3). This was broadly consistent with the movement of the US dollar against most major currencies. As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the real effective exchange rate index, the real effective exchange rate index of the Hong Kong dollar continued to track closely the changes in the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Portfolio investment by non-residents recorded inflows in the second half of 2017. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that equity securities investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter, reflecting improved regional economic outlook and optimistic market sentiment (Table 4.A). Non-residents' investment in debt securities recorded inflows in the third quarter of 2017, offsetting outflows from residents' debt investment. A survey of global mutual funds also indicated that both equity and debt investments recorded inflows in the fourth quarter of 2017, driven by optimism over economic outlook and firms' earnings. In recent weeks, survey data showed that equity investments continued to record inflows despite corrections in global financial markets, while bond investment recorded slight capital outflows (Chart 4.4). Chart 4.4 Market Survey on Equity and Bond-related Capital Flows Looking ahead, as US monetary policy normalisation continues, the negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar will widen, which may lead to increased arbitrage activities. Therefore, the possibility of the weak-side CU being triggered should not be ruled out. This is a normal process under the LERS. Meanwhile, given the uncertain pace of US monetary policy normalisation and the rapidly changing global macro financial conditions and market sentiment, volatility in HKD funds flows and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may increase. The HKMA will continue to fully guarantee the stability of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate in accordance with the Currency Board mechanism. Despite the Federal Reserve raising interest rates and continuing to reduce its balance sheet, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2017 and recently. The HKD Monetary Base rose further by 1.4% in the second half of 2017, driven mainly by growth in Certificates of Indebtedness issued for the backing of banknotes (Chart 4.5). As the CUs were not triggered, the aggregate balance and the outstanding amount of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes remained broadly unchanged in the second half at around HK$1,226.8 billion. Within this, the aggregate balance decreased while outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased correspondingly. This was due to additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills (totalling HK$80 billion) to meet substantial demand from banks for liquidity management purposes. Entering 2018, the Monetary Base remained stable despite a correction in the stock market. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base Meanwhile, Hong Kong dollar money supply grew further in the second half of 2017, though at a slower pace. Growth in Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) moderated from 8.9% in the first half to 2.5% in the second half. Hong Kong dollar deposits, the major component of HKD M3, rose slightly by 2.2% in the second half (Chart 4.7). Among these, demand deposits grew more rapidly in the second half, partly due to buoyant asset markets and increased investment demand. Analysis of counterpart assets showed that growth in HKD M3 was supported on one hand by strong growth in Hong Kong dollar loans (Chart 4.6), and was dragged down on the other hand by net outflows of HKD funds from the non-bank private sector and contraction in banks' net foreign currency assets. Chart 4.6 Changes in HKD M3 and Its Counterpart Assets On the other hand, foreign currency deposits growth was mixed. Partly reflecting currency depreciation of the US dollar against most major currencies, the growth rate of US dollar deposits fell from 3.0% in the first half to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits, after declining continuously for more than two years, rebounded significantly in the second half by 8.4%. This was mainly driven by a recent recovery in renminbi deposits. Due to slower growth in Hong Kong dollar deposits and US dollar deposits, total deposits of AIs increased slightly by 3.0% in the second half, compared with 5.6% in the first half. For 2017 as a whole, total deposits grew moderately by 8.7%, broadly similar to 2016. Chart 4.7 Deposit Growth During September to December 2017, increased funding demand from IPO activities and banks' prudent approach to manage their liquidity ahead of month-end and year-end exerted upward pressure on HKD interbank interest rates (Chart 4.8). Compared with six months earlier, overnight and three-month HIBORs rose by 14 and 50 basis points respectively, reaching 0.25% and 1.26% in December (on a monthly average basis). The negative interest rate differential between one-month to three-month HKD and USD HIBORs narrowed correspondingly. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD Interbank Interest Rates Meanwhile, the Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted upward but flattened, broadly in line with the movement of the US dollar yield curve. In the second half, the three-year Hong Kong Government bond yields rose by 63 basis points, closing at 1.52% at end-2017, while the 10-year Hong Kong Government bond yields rose by a smaller margin of 33 basis points, closing at 1.83% at end-2017 (Chart 4.9). Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate and New Mortgage Average Lending Rate Entering 2018, the Hong Kong dollar interbank market continued to operate in an orderly manner. As year-end funding demand subsided, HKD interbank interest rates fell back in early January. Thereafter, HKD interbank interest rates remained broadly stable despite corrections in global and local stock markets. Overnight and three-month HIBORs stood at 0.43% and 1.08% respectively at end-February 2018. At the retail level, while banks' lending rates rose in tandem with higher HIBORs, the cost of funding for banks generally remained low due to the still-ample deposit base. Despite keen competition in the mortgage lending business, banks' new mortgage average lending rate gradually increased by 36 basis points to 2.16% in December (Chart 4.9), broadly following the rise in one-month HIBORs. On the other hand, the composite interest rate, which measures the cost of funding of retail banks' Hong Kong dollar funding, rose briefly in October due to increased funding demand from IPO activities, but remained subdued for most of the second half, closing at 0.38% at end-December. Looking ahead, as US monetary policy continues to normalise, coupled with the possibility that other major economies may initiate interest rate normalisation, HKD interest rates may face greater upward pressure. At the same time, fluctuating global market sentiment and rapidly changing macro financial conditions may increase volatility in capital flows. However, the sizeable HKD Monetary Base provides a buffer to help cushion any sharp rise in HKD interest rates. In addition, prudent liquidity management by banks and access to discounting at the discount window also help contain excessive volatility in interbank interest rates. Bank credit grew strongly throughout 2017. Loan growth was as high as 10.2% in the first half, moderating to 5.3% in the second half (Chart 4.10). Both loans for use in Hong Kong and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew at a slower pace in the second half of 2017. Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans continued to grow rapidly by 9.5% in the second half, supported by a favourable domestic economic environment and relatively low Hong Kong dollar cost of funding, while foreign currency loans rose only marginally by 0.1%. Among these, growth in US dollar loans moderated to 1.8%, partly due to rising US dollar cost of funding. For 2017 as a whole, total lending recorded strong growth of 16.1%, compared with 6.5% in 2016. Chart 4.10 Loan Growth Growth in domestic loans (including trade finance) moderated from 9.4% in the first half to 5.6% in the second half, with mixed performance across major sectors (Chart 4.11). Loan growth for construction and property development and investment slowed in the second half, partly because banks were required to strengthen their risk management of loans to property developers from June 2017 onwards. Despite further improvements in merchandise trade and retail sales, trade finance and transportation sector loans recorded only relatively modest growth, while wholesale and retail sector loans declined. In contrast, loans to financial and financial-related enterprises remained robust, reflecting in part the steady expansion of the financial services sector. Chart 4.11 Domestic Loan Growth by Sector Household debt grew by 6.5% in the second half of 2017, compared with 5.0% growth in the first half. Within household debt, growth in personal loans (including credit card advances and other loans for personal use) accelerated further, rising by 12.4% in the second half. The strong growth in personal loans was mainly driven by borrowing by private banking and wealth management customers with financial assets as collateral. The growth in these loans was broadly in line with the continued growth in customer assets managed by banks. The risk associated with such collateralised loans is manageable. In addition, the HKMA issued guidelines to banks in January 2014 on risk management of personal loans, requiring banks to adopt prudent risk management measures, including capping loan tenor and borrowers' debt-servicing ratios. On the other hand, despite an increase in residential transaction volumes, the LTV ratio of newly approved mortgages declined, and residential mortgage loan growth eased slightly to 3.8% in the second half. Overall, the household debt-to-GDP ratio rose from 68.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 70.2% in the fourth quarter (Chart 4.12).

Benefiting mainly from growth in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks improved in the second half of 2017 compared with the same period in 2016. Capital and liquidity positions remained sound. Loan growth, after experiencing strong growth in the first half of 2017, slowed in the second half, while asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Despite a significant rise in HKD interbank interest rates, the cost of HKD funds for retail banks remained low due to low retail deposit rates. However, banks should be alert to the risks of rising interest rate volatility and possible outflows of funds under US monetary policy normalisation, as well as geopolitical risks. Given persistently rising corporate leverage and high levels of personal indebtedness, banks should assess the possible impact on asset quality should interest rates rise more than expected. To enhance banks' resilience against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio in Hong Kong will be raised to 2.5% from 1 January 2019. In the second half of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks increased by 13.6% compared with the same period a year earlier. This was mainly attributable to a significant increase in net interest income and a decline in loan impairment charges, which more than offset the decrease in non-interest income. However, as asset growth outpaced profit growth, the return on assets of retail banks edged down slightly from 1.17% in the first half to 1.15% in the second half of 2017. Nevertheless, the return on assets in the second half of 2017 remained higher than the 1.11% recorded in the same period of 2016 (Chart 5.1). For the full year of 2017, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 15.8%, while the return on assets rose from 1.09% in 2016 to 1.16%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks The net interest margin of retail banks widened further from 1.34% in the fourth quarter of 2016 to 1.5% in the fourth quarter of 2017 (Chart 5.2). Anecdotal evidence suggests that the improvement in net interest margins is consistent with rising average spreads on HKD corporate loans in the Hong Kong syndicated loan market (Chart 5.3). Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Chart 5.3 Average spread of HKD syndicated loans HIBORs rose broadly from September 2017, driven mainly by IPO-related and year-end liquidity demand from banks, as well as expectations of US interest rate hikes. In particular, the three-month HIBOR reached a post-financial crisis high of 1.31% at end-December 2017, up 53 basis points from end-June, though it remained low by historical standards (blue line in Chart 5.4). Into 2018, HIBORs appeared to have stabilised as banks' year-end liquidity demand eased. Despite the recent rise in HIBORs, the cost of HKD funds for retail banks remained stable. This was mainly due to low retail deposit rates during the review period. Against this backdrop, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, stayed at a low level of around 0.3% for most of the second half of 2017, before edging up slightly to 0.38% at end-December (green line in Chart 5.4). A similar pattern was observed in the overall HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong. In the second half of 2017, the average HKD and USD non-deposit market funding costs of banks rose by 35 basis points, while the average deposit funding costs rose slightly by 12 basis points. Overall, the average total HKD and USD funding costs of licensed banks rose by 22 basis points (red line in Chart 5.5). Chart 5.4 Interest rates Chart 5.5 HKD and USD funding costs and tenor of licensed banks The rise in HIBORs exceeded the increase in overall funding costs of the Hong Kong banking sector, which could help improve the spreads on banks' HIBOR-based assets. However, this improvement may be partly offset by keen competition in the mortgage market. In particular, market information indicates that some banks have lowered the spread between their mortgage rates and the benchmark rate, or offered fixed-rate mortgage terms to attract new customers. Given expectations of further US interest rate hikes this year, banks may soon face greater upward pressure on funding costs. With keen competition in the loan market, if rising funding costs cannot be fully passed on to customers, this could put pressure on banks' net interest margins. The consolidated capital adequacy ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained well above international minimum requirements, indicating that the Hong Kong banking sector maintains a robust capital base. At end-December 2017, the total capital ratio increased from 18.7% at end-June to 19.1% (Chart 5.6), while the Tier 1 capital ratio54 also rose to 16.6%, of which 15.4% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.55 Chart 5.6 Capital of locally incorporated authorized institutions The HKMA recently published a consultation paper to consult on rules for developing loss-absorbing capacity requirements for authorized institutions under the Financial Institutions (Resolution) Ordinance. While enhancing the loss-absorbing capacity of authorized institutions would benefit society by reducing the likelihood of financial crises, it would inevitably entail costs. Feature 5 presents a cost-benefit assessment of the potential impact of loss-absorbing capacity requirements on Hong Kong. Our assessment indicates that implementing loss-absorbing capacity requirements would bring a net benefit to the Hong Kong economy. As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirements under Basel III, liquidity conditions in the banking sector remained sound during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 144.2% in the second quarter of 2017 to 155.1% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 80% applicable in 2017. Although the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions edged down slightly from 49.7% in the second quarter of 2017 to 49.4% in the fourth quarter, it remained well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. The ample liquidity of authorized institutions demonstrates the ability of the Hong Kong banking sector to withstand liquidity shocks arising from possible outflows of funds from Hong Kong. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the Basel III liquidity standards, was implemented in Hong Kong on 1 January 2018. The requirement aims to reduce the medium- to long-term funding risk of banks by requiring them to maintain sufficient stable sources of funding to finance their business activities. Specifically, category 1 institutions must maintain a Net Stable Funding Ratio of no less than 100% at all times.57 Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting a stable funding structure for the banking system. At end-December 2017, the proportion of Customer deposits to total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained largely unchanged compared with six months earlier, staying at 56.2% (Chart 5.8). Chart 5.8 Liability structure of all authorized institutions The loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions in HKD rose from 77.1% at end-June 2017 to 82.7% at end-December (Chart 5.9), reflecting faster growth in HKD loan and advances compared with deposits during the review period. Meanwhile, as foreign currency deposits grew faster than loans, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell from 65.5% at end-June 2017 to 63.1% at end-December. Overall, the loan-to-deposit ratio in all currencies rose from 71.4% six months earlier to 73.0%. Banks should assess the impact of rising loan-to-deposit ratios on their ability to manage their liquidity. Chart 5.9 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained low. We estimate that under a hypothetical shock of a 200-basis-point rise in interest rates across the board, the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks could decline by an amount equivalent to 3.45% of their total capital base as at end-December 2017 (Chart 5.10). Nonetheless, given expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue to raise interest rates and proceed with balance sheet normalisation, banks should assess the implications for their interest rate risk management. Chart 5.10 Impact of interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks In the second half of 2017, against a moderate but still favourable economic environment, the growth of total loans and advances of all authorized institutions slowed from the strong growth of 10.2% recorded in the first half to 5.3%. After two years of slowdown, total lending grew robustly by 16.1% for the full year of 2017. The asset quality of banks' loan portfolio remained sound and continued to improve in the second half of 2017. At end-December 2017, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions declined to 0.67% and 0.52% respectively, compared with 0.84% and 0.61% at end-June. For retail banks, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans also fell to 0.54% and 0.4% respectively (Chart 5.11). However, given the rapid growth of loans used outside Hong Kong in recent years, banks' asset quality may be more susceptible to the external environment, and banks should therefore closely monitor their credit risk. Chart 5.11 Asset quality of retail banks As banks' expectations about near-term loan growth became more optimistic, strong loan growth is expected to continue. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook in December 2017 showed that 29% of surveyed authorized institutions expected loan demand to increase over the next three months, while the remaining 71% expected loan demand to remain unchanged (Table 5.A). Credit risk in personal lending remained low during the review period. Banks' mortgage loan portfolio remained sound, with the delinquency ratio staying at a low level of 0.03% at end-December 2017. The average LTV ratio of newly approved mortgages declined further from 50.1% in the second quarter of 2017 to 48.8% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.12). This LTV ratio is well below the 64% recorded before the HKMA implemented the first round of countercyclical macroprudential measures (i.e. September 2009).

The global economy continued to expand, but growth momentum moderated amid heightened uncertainty stemming from persistent trade tensions, tighter financial conditions, and other idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds. The Federal Reserve adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that policy decisions would be "data-dependent" and that "patience" was warranted, leading investors to rule out the possibility of further rate hikes. Nevertheless, financial markets may become more sensitive to forthcoming data releases, particularly those that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. In Hong Kong, despite the weak-side CU being triggered in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. In the second half of 2018, total lending growth edged down slightly, reflecting reduced credit demand amid the ongoing China-US trade conflict and slowing global economic growth. The residential property market also cooled in the second half of 2018, with a notable decline in transaction volumes and a pullback in property prices, before showing signs of stabilisation in early 2019. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector faces multiple headwinds from increased uncertainty in the external environment. Should these uncertainties intensify and persist, they could significantly dampen business sentiment and credit demand, thereby exerting downward pressures on banks' profitability. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should prudently assess the potential deterioration of the external environment and its impact on the credit risk associated with their corporate loan portfolios. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to grow. However, while the US economy expanded robustly, growth momentum in other regions moderated. Among advanced economies, Japan and several major euro area countries slowed, with inflation remaining low. A deceleration in global trade and a sharp fall in oil prices posed cyclical headwinds to emerging market economies. In light of softening global growth momentum, the International Monetary Fund downgraded its global growth forecasts for 2019 and 2020 in January by 0.2 and 0.1 percentage points respectively compared with its October 2018 projections. Amid a dimming growth outlook and escalating trade tensions, global equity markets experienced significant volatility at end-2018. US Central Government bond yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the Global Financial Crisis, raising concerns about an impending US recession. Nonetheless, US economic fundamentals remained sound, and the likelihood of a near-term recession was low. That said, the global economic outlook remains fraught with uncertainty. In the US, while moderate inflation gives the Federal Reserve room to pause rate hikes, the data-dependent nature of its monetary policy also suggests that financial markets may become more sensitive to forthcoming data, particularly those that could prompt monetary policy tightening, such as a rise in US inflation. Meanwhile, the outcomes of trade negotiations between the US and China, as well as between the US and the EU, remain uncertain. In the UK, whether an arrangement to avoid a "hard Brexit" can be achieved remains to be seen. In East Asia, financial markets have stabilised as the US dollar's appreciation slowed and markets anticipated a pause in Federal Reserve rate hikes, but a deteriorating external environment could weigh on regional economic growth. Indeed, the weakening of global trade growth momentum has already dragged on the economic growth of several East Asian economies, while inflationary pressures have also eased. While this development may alleviate the policy dilemma faced by regional central banks between supporting growth and containing inflation, financial imbalances such as high private sector debt in some economies in the region remain acute. As discussed in Feature 1 (page 16), another challenge facing East Asia is the potential spillover to sovereign bond market of emerging market economies (including East Asian economies) should the Federal Reserve's monetary policy shift in an unexpected direction. In Mainland China, growth slowed further in the second half of 2018, owing to heightened external uncertainty and a modest softening in domestic demand. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains uncertain pending the outcome of China-US trade negotiations. The significant contraction in shadow financing activities has increased financing difficulties for private enterprises—particularly smaller firms—over the past several quarters, and weakening economic confidence could also weigh on business activity. In this challenging economic environment, policymakers need to continue striking a balance between stabilising the economy and guarding against potential systemic risks through accommodative but targeted measures, such as targeted reserve requirement ratio cuts. At the same time, authorities have implemented additional supply-side measures to boost productivity growth—for instance, by promoting competition among firms of different ownership types—and to provide better social safety nets for individuals. The official growth target for 2019 has also been lowered from around 6.5% in 2018 to a range of 6.0% to 6.5%. In 2018, risk aversion dominated Mainland financial markets. Banks' asset quality deteriorated slightly during the review period, while the leverage of listed corporates in the non-financial sector edged up modestly. Nonetheless, loan impairment charges continued to increase in the second half of 2018, and banks' exposure to off-balance sheet wealth management products continued to decline—both developments helping to shield the banking system from potential deterioration in credit quality. Another positive development was that the leverage of listed corporates in overcapacity sectors—one of the key sources of banks' credit risk—declined further in the first three quarters of 2018. Feature 2 (page 32) provides an in-depth analysis of the factors contributing to the recent improvement in the performance of overcapacity sectors. Hong Kong's economic activity softened in the second half of 2018 compared with the first half. Quarter-on-quarter GDP growth stalled, and year-on-year growth also slowed, dragging full-year economic growth down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. The weakening of economic activity was mainly attributable to the direct and indirect impact of the China-US trade conflict on private consumption and exports of goods. The slowdown in private consumption may reflect heightened economic uncertainty and the negative wealth effect from adjustments in local asset prices. On the external front, Hong Kong's exports of goods also underperformed, particularly following the imposition of additional tariffs by both China and the US in the fourth quarter. Feature 3 examines more closely the impact of the China-US trade conflict on Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance, and discusses the near-term outlook and associated risks. Largely due to slowing global economic growth, economic growth is expected to moderate further in 2019. Under the influence of multiple interacting factors, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. Domestically, private consumption is expected to continue supporting economic growth amid low unemployment and rising household incomes, although the outlook for aggregate investment spending may become more uncertain. The government has forecast real GDP growth of 2% to 3% for 2019, while the latest average forecast from private sector analysts stands at 2.3%. These forecasts are subject to the various uncertainties and risks described above. Local inflation edged up slightly in the second half of 2018 but remained moderate. The modest increase was partly driven by growth in newly signed residential rentals. Meanwhile, while the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8%—the lowest level in over 20 years—there were signs of a slowdown in total employment growth. Looking ahead, as local economic growth momentum weakens, local inflationary pressures are expected to remain moderate in 2019. Following the triggering of the weak-side CU in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate moved away from 7.8500, trading between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until the weak-side CU was triggered again four times in March 2019 (up to 19 March). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose in September and November, partly reflecting the unwinding of carry trade positions amid tighter liquidity conditions. Into 2019, the Hong Kong dollar weakened against the US dollar, partly due to the re-establishment of carry trade positions. Despite the weak-side CU being triggered again in March, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. As a result of the weak-side CU being triggered, the aggregate balance declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). HKD interbank interest rates rose broadly in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting expectations of US rate hikes. Compared with June 2018, the 3-month and 12-month HIBORs rose by around 30 basis points each to 2.32% and 2.74% respectively in December (on a monthly average basis). Into 2019, HKD interbank interest rates declined overall as seasonal demand eased. The composite interest rate, which measures the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks, rose from 0.62% at end-June 2018 to 0.83% at end-January 2019. In response to higher cost of funding, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points following the upward adjustment in the target range for the US federal funds rate at end-September. At end-January 2019, the average lending rate on new mortgage loans rose to approximately 2.45%, in line with the increase in Best Lending Rates. Given persistent uncertainties relating to China-US trade tensions and Brexit negotiations, capital flow volatility may intensify. Furthermore, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and its USD counterparts could stimulate carry trade activity, leading to capital outflows. Under such circumstances, capital outflows and the potential triggering of the weak-side CU are normal operations under the LERS. Since the beginning of 2018, both CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates came under depreciation pressure amid market concerns over escalating China-US trade tensions. However, buoyed by optimism stemming from the resumption of high-level trade talks between China and the US, both CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November. Despite the continued China-US trade tensions, they have not yet had any significant impact on funding conditions in the CNH interbank market. Overnight CNH HIBOR remained below 4% for most of 2018, while the 3-month CNH rate hovered around 4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of the year, with RMB customer deposits growing by 5.2% in the second half of 2018. The daily average turnover of the RMB RTGS system remained at elevated levels, rising further to RMB1,010.1 billion in 2018. Despite lingering concerns over China-US trade tensions, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to continue to expand, driven by the liberalisation of the Mainland's capital account, the development of stock and bond connect schemes, and regional economic cooperation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives. The local equity markets experienced a rollercoaster ride over the past six months. In the early part of the review period, markets fell sharply due to continued tightening of US monetary policy, significant divergences in the China-US trade negotiations, and increasing signs of weakening economic growth on the Mainland. Subsequently, as the US economic outlook weakened and became more uncertain, the Federal Reserve shifted to a "patient" monetary policy stance. At the same time, during the trade war truce period, China took additional measures to reduce its trade surplus with the US and to open its markets to foreign investors. While the US brought highly politicised legal proceedings against a Chinese telecommunications company, both sides displayed goodwill and demonstrated resolve to reach a trade agreement. Against this backdrop, local equity markets rebounded sharply at the start of the year. However, as both sides discuss the details of any potential agreement, considerable uncertainty remains ahead, and the future development of the US federal prosecution is likely to complicate matters further, particularly in the high-technology sector. The local Hong Kong dollar debt market grew slightly last year. Yields declined, and as market expectations for a slower pace of normalisation of US monetary policy strengthened towards year-end, performance improved. As a result, capital flows into bond funds reversed course and increased modestly in the second half. Issuance in Hong Kong's offshore renminbi market rebounded strongly after three consecutive years of decline. However, as Mainland companies continued to deleverage, total issuance remained below the amount of maturing debt. Looking ahead, the local debt market faces continued challenges, and its prospects hinge on global—and particularly Mainland—economic developments.

During the review period, the global economy continued to expand, but growth momentum moderated under the combined influence of idiosyncratic and cyclical headwinds, particularly outside the United States. In light of the dimming growth outlook, the Fed adjusted its monetary policy stance, emphasising that its decisions would be "data-dependent" and that "patience" was warranted, and stopped providing forward guidance on further interest rate hikes. As the Fed's policy inclination becomes data-dependent, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data releases and may perceive monetary policy as more uncertain. Meanwhile, heightened uncertainty surrounding global trade policies and geopolitical risks may continue to cast a shadow over the global growth outlook. In East Asia, financial markets have largely stabilised since late 2018, as signs emerged that the US interest rate hike cycle was slowing and the US dollar steadied. Nevertheless, the region may face a broad-based slowdown given the deteriorating external environment—namely, the unresolved China-US trade conflict and weakening growth in advanced economies. In Mainland China, growth drivers moderated further in the second half of 2018, and uncertainty over the growth outlook rose amid the China-US trade conflict and financing difficulties faced by small enterprises. Policymakers therefore adopted more targeted measures to stabilise the economy and support private and small enterprises. Confronting these challenges, policymakers will need to strike a careful balance between continuing to guard against systemic risks and supporting businesses and the real economy. In the second half of 2018, the global economy continued to expand broadly. However, while the US economy remained broadly resilient, some signs of slowdown emerged. There were also clear signs of easing growth momentum outside the United States. A number of country-specific shocks—including natural disasters in Japan, the introduction of new automobile emission standards in Germany, a sharp rise in Italian Central Government bond yields amid a fiscal standoff with the EU, and social unrest in France—all weighed on economic activity in advanced economies (Figure 2.1). In addition, a cyclical slowdown in global import growth acted as a drag on industrial production in emerging market economies (Figure 2.2). The sharp drop in oil prices in Q4 also posed new challenges for emerging market economies that export commodities. In light of the moderation in growth momentum in the second half of 2018, the International Monetary Fund lowered its 2019 global economic growth forecast by 0.2 percentage points to 3.5% in January. Figure 2.1 Composite PMI for Selected Advanced Economies Figure 2.2 Global Import Volume and Industrial Production in Emerging Market Economies In Q4, global equity markets underwent a significant correction amid slowing global growth momentum, heightened trade policy uncertainty, concerns over the sustainability of US firms' earnings growth, and the Fed's signals that monetary policy tightening would continue. As financial market sentiment deteriorated, the US Central Government bond yield curve flattened to levels not seen since the Global Financial Crisis, prompting some market participants to worry about an impending US recession (Figure 2.3). Figure 2.3 Spread between 10-year and 3-month US Central Government Bond Yields and Implied Probability of a US Recession Nonetheless, the probability of a near-term US recession remains low. US economic fundamentals remain solid, particularly the tight labour market, which is expected to continue supporting private consumption. At the same time, the US output gap is estimated to have only turned positive last year, reducing the likelihood of the economy overheating and prompting the Fed to tighten monetary policy aggressively. However, possibly in response to the significant tightening of financial conditions since Q4, senior Fed officials began in early January to emphasise that monetary policy would be data-dependent, noting that subdued inflationary pressures gave them room to be "patient" in determining future monetary policy adjustments. In addition, following its January meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee stopped providing forward guidance on further interest rate hikes and announced that it "would be prepared to adjust any of the details for completing balance sheet normalisation in light of economic and financial developments." This shift triggered a rebound in global equity markets (Figure 2.4). Figure 2.4 S&P 500, MSCI World (ex-US) and MSCI Emerging Markets Indices Despite the Fed's recent dovish pivot signals, the outlook for US monetary policy remains highly uncertain and will depend on inflation and other developments. Inflationary pressures have been subdued so far, giving the Fed room to gradually advance monetary normalisation. Inflation expectations have remained stable in recent years, supporting the case for "patience" (Figure 2.5). Moreover, as Fed Chair Powell noted in January, the US economic outlook faces multiple headwinds, including slower growth outside the US and trade policy uncertainty. In light of these developments, the Fed may need to adopt a more cautious monetary policy stance. Figure 2.5 Market-based and Survey-based Measures of US Inflation Expectations Nevertheless, the tight labour market is expected to continue supporting the overall performance of the US economy. In this environment, wage growth may accelerate, which typically signals that inflation could intensify in the future (Figure 2.6). As a result, market expectations that have largely priced out the possibility of a Fed rate hike in 2019 may be overly optimistic (Figure 2.7). Figure 2.6 Average Hourly Earnings and Core PCE Inflation Figure 2.7 Futures-implied Probability of the Federal Funds Rate Target Range Remaining Unchanged or Increasing by at Least One Hike in 2019 In summary, a prolonged pause in Fed rate hikes is by no means certain. To reduce the risk of policy errors, the Fed has increasingly emphasised that its decisions will be data-dependent as a risk management strategy. By implication, financial markets may become more sensitive to incoming data, particularly data that could prompt monetary policy tightening. The monetary policy outlook for other major central banks is also uncertain. In the Euro area, the ECB concluded its asset purchase programme in December while continuing to reinvest in full the principal payments from maturing securities purchased under the programme, and reiterated its forward guidance to keep policy rates unchanged at least through the summer of 2019. However, the ECB downgraded its near-term growth assessment in January, characterising the risks to the growth outlook as "tilted to the downside." The implications of this downward revision in the ECB's economic growth assessment for monetary policy remain to be seen. In Japan, the Bank of Japan indicated at its most recent policy meeting that it would ease its monetary policy stance if necessary in the face of increased downside risks. However, further monetary policy easing may face significant resistance, given that its effectiveness has been questioned and the adverse side-effects of maintaining an ultra-low interest rate environment for an extended period are becoming increasingly apparent—for example, the capital ratios of regional banks have fallen from 10.6% in 2015 to 9.7% in 2018, persistently dragged down by low yields eroding profitability. Consequently, the Bank of Japan has very limited room to adjust monetary policy in the near term. Beyond the uncertainty surrounding the global monetary policy outlook, uncertain outcomes of future trade negotiations and heightened geopolitical risks are two major sources of risk for the global economic outlook. The US government announced in early December that it would not raise tariffs on imports from China for 90 days, and extended this deadline again at the end of February, but whether the two sides can reach a lasting trade agreement remains to be seen. Meanwhile, trade negotiations between the United States and the European Union have made little progress at this stage. The uncertain outcome of these trade negotiations may continue to cloud the global growth outlook. Policy and geopolitical risks are also prominent. In the United States, a disagreement between the two parties over border security funding led to a 35-day federal government shutdown from late December 2018 to late January 2019. While the impact of the shutdown on economic growth should be temporary, the tensions between the Trump administration and the Democrat-controlled House of Representatives may lead to more policy gridlock in the future. In the United Kingdom, risks related to Brexit and its knock-on effects surged after Prime Minister May's Brexit deal was overwhelmingly rejected in mid-January, and it remains unknown whether a solution can be found at the last minute to avoid a disruptive "hard Brexit." Elsewhere, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, such as the reimposition of US sanctions on Iran, may also add uncertainty to oil prices and thereby affect the global growth outlook. In East Asia, financial markets were broadly stable in Q4 after a volatile first three quarters of last year. The stabilisation of the US dollar since October, together with signs that the Fed was prepared to be patient regarding further interest rate hikes, helped ease currency depreciation pressures and fund outflow pressures faced by East Asian economies. Several regional currencies edged up against the US dollar in Q4, and portfolio investment flows returned to net inflows (Figure 2.8). Figure 2.8 East Asia: Currency Indices and Capital Flows Despite the stabilisation in financial markets, there are increasing signs of a broad-based regional slowdown. Weakening global trade momentum caused by the China-US trade conflict led to a decline in export growth in the region, causing real GDP growth to slow in the second half of last year for most East Asian economies. Indeed, the new export orders sub-indices of the PMIs for several regional economies (which reflect near-term external trade performance) fell into contractionary territory from Q4 onwards, signalling that near-term growth momentum may weaken further (Figure 2.9). Figure 2.9 Markit PMI New Export Orders Indices for East Asian Economies Against a backdrop of slowing economic growth and the recent decline in oil prices, inflationary pressures in East Asia have eased (Figure 2.10). Figure 2.10 East Asia: Headline Inflation and Oil Prices With both inflationary pressures and upward pressure on the US dollar remaining relatively subdued recently, there is no pressing need for East Asian central banks to raise interest rates, alleviating the policy dilemma of balancing the promotion of economic growth against the need to contain inflation and fund outflows. However, as private sector debt in some East Asian economies remains elevated by emerging market standards, central banks continue to face the challenge of financial imbalances (Figure 2.11).

Hong Kong's economy softened in the second half of 2018, reflecting slower growth in private consumption and weakening export performance amid the China-US trade conflict. With global economic growth slowing, real GDP growth is expected to moderate in 2019. Hong Kong's growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including trade protectionism, the future direction of US monetary policy, and economic performance in Mainland China. Inflationary pressures in Hong Kong should remain moderate in 2019, though the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. Hong Kong's economic activity softened in the second half of 2018. Specifically, economic activity failed to sustain the strong momentum of the first half, with real GDP growth (in quarter-on-quarter terms) turning slightly negative in the second half (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). On a year-on-year basis, economic growth also slowed, with the growth rate for the fourth quarter at 1.3%, below trend growth, dragging the full-year growth rate down from 3.8% in 2017 to 3.0% in 2018. * Based on seasonally adjusted volume index of real GDP compiled from the expenditure approach. Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions from major expenditure components. The weakening of economic activity was largely due to the drag on consumption and exports from the direct and indirect effects of the China-US trade conflict. Private consumption growth slowed, partly owing to increased economic uncertainties and the wealth effect from domestic asset price corrections (Chart 3.1). Investment spending fell sharply amid fragile business sentiment. Hong Kong's external merchandise trade performance also deteriorated, particularly after both the US and Mainland China implemented additional tariffs in the fourth quarter (Chart 3.2). Nevertheless, as total imports slowed more sharply than total exports, net trade still made a positive contribution to GDP in the fourth quarter. Feature 3 takes a closer look at Hong Kong's merchandise trade performance and examines the near-term outlook and associated risks. Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports. As economic activity weakened, job growth appeared to slow in the second half of 2018. Total employment increased by only 0.1% to around 3,873,000 at the end of 2018, lower than the 0.8% growth in the first half of the year. With output and job growth both subdued, labour productivity remained broadly stable, with no signs of significant improvement. With global economic growth slowing further, Hong Kong's economic growth is expected to moderate in 2019. Facing external headwinds, Hong Kong's export performance is expected to remain under pressure. On the domestic front, while low unemployment rates and rising household incomes will continue to support private consumption, it is expected that private consumption growth will slow, partly due to weakening consumer confidence and the wealth effect from earlier asset price corrections. The outlook for gross fixed capital formation may become more uncertain. While building and construction activities are expected to continue growing steadily with increasing housing supply, businesses may become more cautious about capital investment amid heightened economic uncertainties. Business sentiment indicators such as the Hong Kong Purchasing Managers' Index continue to hover in contractionary territory, and the implied year-on-year growth from this index points to a further slowdown in GDP growth in the near term. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2% and 3% for 2019, while the latest market consensus forecasts from private sector analysts range from 1.5% to 2.7%. Hong Kong's growth outlook is subject to a number of uncertainties and risks as discussed in the previous two chapters. Although inflationary pressures have been building up in recent months, they remain moderate. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters of 2018 respectively, higher than the average increase of 2.4% in the first half of the year. The 3-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also edged up recently, rising from 2.5% in July 2018 to 2.6% in January 2019 (Chart 3.3). The slight pick-up in inflation momentum was driven by increases in certain service prices. The continued pass-through of earlier increases in newly-signed residential rentals and the accelerating rise in dining-out prices continued to push up services inflation (Chart 3.4). However, labour cost pressures in recent quarters remained broadly moderate (Chart 3.5). Chart 3.3 Various indicators of consumer price inflation. Chart 3.4 CPI rental component and market rentals. Chart 3.5 Unit labour cost and per capita wages. Looking ahead, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong should remain moderate in 2019. This mainly reflects the weakening of domestic growth drivers. However, earlier increases in residential rentals will continue to feed through to consumer price inflation. Market consensus forecasts suggest a moderate full-year headline inflation rate of 2.2%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks. On the downside, the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate remains at around 2.8%, its lowest level in over 20 years (Chart 3.6). If the labour market deteriorates unexpectedly, the currently near-zero output gap could turn negative, potentially exerting additional downward pressures on inflation. On the other hand, if the China-US trade tensions ease and the domestic economy outperforms expectations, this could push up domestic inflation. Chart 3.6 Unemployment rate. The China-US trade conflict escalated progressively in the second half of 2018: the US imposed tariffs of 25% on US$34 billion and US$16 billion worth of imports from Mainland China on 6 July and 23 August respectively. In response to these two rounds, Mainland China imposed equivalent tariffs of 25% on equal values of US goods. The US escalated further on 24 September, imposing tariffs of 10% on US$200 billion worth of imports from Mainland China. Mainland China swiftly responded by imposing tariffs of 5% to 10% on US$60 billion worth of US goods. The two sides subsequently entered into negotiations to avoid further tariff escalation. As Hong Kong has traditionally served as an entrepôt between these two economies, the imposition of tariffs will inevitably have a direct impact on Hong Kong through the trade channel. The China-US trade conflict therefore has important implications for Hong Kong's macroeconomic and financial stability. This feature reviews Hong Kong's recent merchandise trade performance and examines its near-term outlook. We also attempt to utilise more granular data to identify the trade goods directly affected by the tariffs in order to examine more closely the impact of the tariff impositions. To analyse the impact of the tariffs, we first extracted data on six groups of Hong Kong re-exports that were affected by the respective rounds of tariffs described in the previous section. In the first two rounds of tariffs, the US primarily targeted capital goods and semi-manufactures, while Mainland China mainly targeted agricultural products, chemicals, medical equipment and energy equipment. In the third round, the range of affected goods expanded to cover more consumer goods. For brevity, we label the goods affected by these three rounds of tariffs as List 1, List 2, and List 3 respectively. After collecting these more granular trade data, we focus on analysing year-on-year changes in the value of Hong Kong re-exports to adjust for seasonal effects. Readers should also exercise caution when interpreting data for September 2018, as trade activity in that month was to some extent disrupted by Super Typhoon Mangkhut. Overall, the analysis in this section should be regarded as preliminary evidence of the tariff impact only. Re-exports of Hong Kong originating from Mainland China and subject to tariffs. Shortly after the tariffs were imposed, re-exports of the relevant goods from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the US appeared to have fallen significantly or seen slower growth (Chart B3.1). For example, the growth in re-exports for List 1 and List 2 slowed in the first month after the tariffs were imposed, while re-exports for List 3 recorded negative growth. In addition, re-exports for all three lists recorded negative growth in December. Chart B3.1 Value of goods re-exported from Mainland China through Hong Kong to the US in 2018. Re-exports of Hong Kong originating from the US and subject to tariffs. In contrast, re-exports of goods from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China showed mixed results (Chart B3.2). Re-exports under List 1 appeared to have declined sharply in the months following the tariff imposition, but rebounded towards the end of the year. Re-exports under List 2 remained broadly in negative growth territory throughout the year, while growth under List 3 appeared broadly stable. Chart B3.2 Value of goods re-exported from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China in 2018. Front-loading. As there is a time lag between the announcement and the eventual implementation of tariffs (or due to the mere threat of tariff imposition), businesses may increase shipments of affected goods ahead of the expected effective date. Indeed, a number of reports and news articles indicate that such front-loading behaviour was fairly widespread. Some private sector analysts also cite this behaviour as a partial explanation for the strong overall trade figures recorded ahead of the tariff impositions. The more granular trade data shows some signs of front-loading in certain tariff list goods, but this appears to be confined to re-exports from Mainland China to the US (Chart B3.1). The growth rates of re-exports for List 1 and List 2 rose in the months leading up to their respective tariff effective dates. On the other hand, the growth rates of re-exports from the US through Hong Kong to Mainland China (Chart B3.2) show no clear signs of front-loading behaviour by businesses. Re-exports of Hong Kong not affected by the tariff impositions. It is worth noting that Hong Kong re-exports (by value) directly affected by the tariff impositions account for only around 4% to 5% of total Hong Kong re-exports. To gain a more complete picture of Hong Kong's trade performance, we should also examine re-exports not affected by the tariff impositions. We found that re-exports not affected by the tariff impositions recorded negative growth in the last two months of 2018 (Chart B3.3). Moreover, the growth in tariff-affected re-exports (red line) has been noticeably more negative since the third quarter, reflecting the significant impact of the tariffs. The slowdown in growth of re-exports not affected by the tariff impositions partly reflects the broader weakening of external demand. As trade tensions continue to generate heightened uncertainties, global financing conditions tighten, and geopolitical risks rise, external demand could come under more broad-based pressure. In particular, the trade conflict has already weighed on global economic sentiment and activity, as reflected in corrections across major equity markets. This has dampened import demand from other economies, thereby suppressing Hong Kong's external trade performance. Chart B3.3 Value of Hong Kong re-exports in 2018. Even if the China-US trade tensions ease, the near-term outlook for Hong Kong's merchandise trade remains challenging. Global economic growth in 2019 is likely to slow (see Chapter 2), which will further weigh on Hong Kong's export performance. Various business sentiment indicators suggest that enterprises of all sizes are pessimistic about their business prospects (Chart B3.4), with business sentiment in the trade sector particularly subdued. Other trade-related industries such as logistics may also be affected. Chart B3.4 Business outlook survey for Hong Kong's import and export sector.

Entering 2019, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually weakened, partly due to corporates repatriating IPO proceeds and the market re-establishing carry trade positions, and the weak-side CU was triggered in March. Nonetheless, Hong Kong dollar trading remained smooth and orderly. HKD interbank interest rates generally rose in the second half of 2018, reflecting expectations of US rate hikes and seasonal funding demand, before retreating in January 2019. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties including ongoing Sino-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, Hong Kong dollar fund flows may become more volatile. If the Hong Kong dollar-US dollar interest rate differential remains wide, carry trade activity in the market may persist, causing the Hong Kong dollar to remain weak for some time and potentially triggering the weak-side CU again, which is consistent with the design of the LERS. Following the triggering of the weak-side CU in late August, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate deviated from 7.8500 and fluctuated between 7.8062 and 7.8499, until the Hong Kong dollar triggered the weak-side CU again a total of four times in March 2019 (as of 19 March) (Chart 4.1). The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate rose briefly in September, partly reflecting carry trade unwinding amid tightened liquidity, but subsequently declined gradually in October. The Hong Kong dollar stabilised again after November, as year-end funding demand tightened liquidity, leading to carry trade unwinding. Despite the triggering of the weak-side CU, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. The Aggregate Balance has remained at around HK$76 billion since August (Chart 4.2), and declined slightly to HK$70.9 billion following the triggering of the weak-side CU in March (as of 19 March).
