As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and thus had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly followed the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates. The latest balance of payments statistics showed that portfolio investment continued to record outflows in the third quarter of 2018. Against a backdrop of weak market sentiment and heightened volatility in equity markets, portfolio investment outflows in equity securities by residents accelerated, more than offsetting non-resident portfolio investment inflows in the third quarter (Table 4.A). In contrast, debt securities investment by both residents and non-residents recorded inflows in the third quarter. Looking ahead, amid uncertainties including ongoing Sino-US trade tensions, Brexit negotiations, and the increasingly unpredictable pace of US monetary policy normalisation, fund flow volatility may intensify. In addition, the significant negative interest rate differential between the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar may stimulate carry trade activity, leading to fund outflow. Under the LERS, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate may weaken and the weak-side CU may be triggered again. Fund outflows and the potential triggering of the weak-side CU are normal operations under the LERS. Despite the ongoing US interest rate normalisation process and the multiple triggering of the weak-side CU between April and August, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2018. The HKD Monetary Base contracted slightly by 0.7% in the second half of the year, reaching HK$1,632.9 billion at end-2018 (Chart 4.4). The contraction in the monetary base was mainly attributable to the triggering of the weak-side CU in August 2018, which caused the Aggregate Balance to decline from HK$109.5 billion at end-June 2018 to HK$76.4 billion at end-2018, while Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased slightly. The HKD Monetary Base remained broadly stable in the first two months of 2019, with the Aggregate Balance showing no significant change since August. Subsequently, following the triggering of the weak-side CU in March, the Aggregate Balance declined slightly to around HK$70.9 billion (as of 19 March). Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base. As for the broader Hong Kong dollar money supply indicators, money supply growth generally slowed in the second half of the year, partly reflecting increased uncertainties in the macroeconomic and financial conditions. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.6% in the first half of the year but only marginally by 0.1% in the second half (Chart 4.5). Hong Kong dollar deposits, as the main component of HKD M3, showed little change compared with end-June (Chart 4.6). Among Hong Kong dollar deposits, demand deposits and savings deposits declined, partly due to reduced investment-related transactions in the second half of the year; on the other hand, time deposits continued to record strong growth as deposit rates were raised. Counterpart analysis showed that HKD M3 growth slowed due to movements in banks' capital and reserves (included in "net other items"). Chart 4.5 Changes in HKD M3 and its Counterparts. Foreign currency deposits grew at a faster pace in the second half of the year. As banks raised their preferential deposit rates for US dollars and attracted more deposits, US dollar deposits grew strongly by 8.8% in the second half, becoming the main driver of foreign currency deposit growth (Chart 4.6). Other foreign currency deposits increased marginally by 1.4% in the second half, with renminbi deposits continuing to record growth. Overall, total deposits of AIs grew moderately by 3.3% in the second half, slightly faster than the 1.6% growth in the first half. Chart 4.6 Deposit Growth. Despite the HKD Monetary Base and deposit levels remaining large, HKD interbank interest rates began to face some upward pressure in the second half of 2018, mainly reflecting US rate hikes. Seasonal liquidity demand occasionally pushed up short-term HIBORs, making them more volatile than longer-term HIBORs (Chart 4.7). The three-month and 12-month HIBORs averaged 2.32% and 2.74% in December, respectively, about 30 basis points higher than the June averages. Entering 2019, HKD interbank interest rates generally declined as seasonal demand subsided. The three-month and 12-month HIBORs fell to averages of 1.65% and 2.39%, respectively, in February. Chart 4.7 HKD and USD Interbank Interest Rates. The Hong Kong dollar yield curve shifted downward in the second half of 2018, broadly tracking movements in the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2018, the 3-year and 10-year Hong Kong Government bond yields fell by 45 and 37 basis points, respectively, to 1.56% and 1.83% at end-February 2019 (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate and New Mortgage Average Lending Rate. During the review period, the composite interest rate, which measures the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funding for retail banks, rose slightly. Reflecting changes in interbank and deposit cost of funding, the composite interest rate rose from 0.62% at end-June to 0.89% at end-December 2018, before declining to 0.83% at end-January 2019 (Chart 4.8). In view of rising cost of funding, following the upward adjustment of the US federal funds rate target range in September, retail banks raised their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 to 25.0 basis points. After the US federal funds rate target range was raised again in December, retail banks did not make further adjustments to their Best Lending Rates. On the other hand, the new mortgage average lending rate rose in line with the Best Lending Rates, standing at around 2.45% at end-January 2019. Looking ahead, the interest rate trajectory of the US dollar, fund flows, and local financial markets activities (such as IPO subscription activities) will continue to be the main drivers of HKD interest rates. Given that the HKD Monetary Base remains large and the banking system holds a substantial amount of Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, which banks can use as collateral to borrow HKD funds through the Discount Window, the pace of increase in HKD interest rates should be relatively moderate. Against the backdrop of escalating Sino-US trade tensions, the CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates have depreciated against the US dollar since the beginning of 2018 (Chart 4.9). However, buoyed by optimism following the resumption of high-level trade negotiations between China and the US, the CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates stabilised in November. Meanwhile, the spread between the onshore renminbi and CNH was not significant during the review period. Chart 4.9 Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates. At present, ongoing Sino-US trade tensions have not had a significant impact on funding positions in the offshore interbank market. As liquidity conditions remained broadly stable, the overnight CNH HIBOR stayed below 4% for most of the review period, rising occasionally only due to seasonal factors (Chart 4.10). The three-month CNH HIBOR hovered around 4% between September and December 2018, before falling to 3.02% at end-February 2019, possibly reflecting recent monetary easing measures by the PBoC. Nonetheless, the impact of the progress of Sino-US trade negotiations on liquidity conditions in the offshore interbank market in 2019 remains to be seen. Chart 4.10 Overnight and Three-month CNH HIBOR Pricing. Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool expanded steadily in the second half of 2018. The combined balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a slightly faster pace than the 2.6% growth in the first half, rising by 3.7% in the second half to RMB657.7 billion at end-2018 (Chart 4.11 and Table 4.B). This was mainly driven by RMB customer deposits, which grew by 4.5% in the first half and 5.2% in the second half. Among these, corporate customer deposits grew faster than individual customer deposits. However, the balance of certificates of deposit declined further by 14.1% in the second half, mainly due to reduced issuance of certificates of deposit and a relatively large amount of certificates of deposit maturing in October.

Benefiting mainly from an increase in net interest income, the profitability of retail banks continued to improve in the second half of 2018 compared with the same period in 2017. Capital and liquidity positions also remained solid. Reflecting the upward pressure on HKD interbank interest rates and retail deposit rates amid US interest rate normalisation, the overall HKD funding costs of retail banks rose significantly but remained at a low level. Against a backdrop of external uncertainties, bank credit contracted moderately in the second half of 2018. Nonetheless, credit growth has shown signs of stabilisation since November, and asset quality remained sound by historical standards. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will face multiple headwinds from continued uncertainty over China-US trade relations, global economic slowdown, uncertain pace of the US monetary policy tightening cycle, and geopolitical risks. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage, banks should remain vigilant about the potential impact on their credit risk of loans to corporates should the external environment deteriorate further.  The overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 14.3% compared with the same period in 2017, while return on assets rose from 1.14% to 1.23% (Chart 5.1). This strong performance was mainly driven by a substantial increase in net interest income, which was sufficient to offset the increase in loan impairment charges and operating expenses. For the full year of 2018, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 19.4%, while return on assets rose from 1.16% in 2017 to 1.27%.  Chart 5.1 Retail bank profitability  The net interest margin of retail banks widened further to 1.67% in the fourth quarter, compared with 1.5% in the same period a year ago (Chart 5.2).  Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks  Largely reflecting further US rate hikes and a decline in interbank HKD liquidity following the triggering of the weak-side CU in August 2018, Hong Kong interbank funding costs continued to face upward pressure in the second half of 2018. Specifically, the three-month HIBORs rose by 23 basis points in the second half of 2018 (Chart 5.3). HKD retail deposit rates also rose during the review period as banks generally raised time deposit rates to attract stable long-term funding. In addition, following the US rate increase decided at end-September, banks raised their Best Lending Rates and correspondingly raised their savings deposits rates. With wholesale and retail funding costs both rising, the Composite Interest Rate — a measure of the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks — rose from 0.62% in June 2018 to 0.89% in December, but remained low by historical standards.  Chart 5.3 Interest rates (a) End-of-period figures. (b) Period average figures for newly approved loans.  On a broader level, the overall HKD and USD funding costs of Hong Kong licensed banks continued to trend upward. In the second half of 2018, the average overall HKD and USD funding costs of banks rose by 36 basis points, compared with an increase of 40 basis points in the first half (the red line in Chart 5.4).  Chart 5.4 HKD and USD funding costs and tenor of licensed banks  The cumulative increase in HIBORs exceeded the rise in the overall funding costs of Hong Kong banks, which may have had a positive impact on retail banks' HIBOR-based mortgage loans, a type of loan that the industry had been actively promoting in recent years. However, future improvements in net interest margins may become more limited, as most HIBOR-based mortgage loans have already reached the cap rate benchmarked against Best Lending Rates. Given the uncertain timing of future increases in Best Lending Rates, the continued upward trend in banks' funding costs amid US interest rate normalisation may weigh on overall net interest margins. Looking ahead, increased uncertainty in the external environment may cast a shadow over banks' earnings outlook. In particular, continued uncertainty over China-US trade relations against a backdrop of slowing global economic growth may dampen business confidence and reduce credit demand for bank lending. Should this lead to a significant decline in loans and a deterioration in asset quality, it could weigh on banks' profitability.  The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remains strong, well above international minimum standards. At end-2018, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.3% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 17.9%, of which 16.0% was Common Equity Tier 1 capital.  Chart 5.5 Capital of locally incorporated authorized institutions 1. Consolidated position. 2. With effect from 1 January 2013, locally incorporated authorized institutions are required to comply with the revised capital framework under Basel III. Accordingly, capital ratios from March 2013 onwards are not directly comparable with data up to December 2012.  In addition to risk-based capital adequacy ratios, Basel III also introduces a non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement to constrain excessive leverage in the banking system. The minimum leverage ratio requirement took effect in Hong Kong in 2018, and the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.0% at end-December 2018, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6).  Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions  As measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained solid during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions rose from 156.6% in the second quarter of 2018 to 167.6% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum of 90% applicable in 2018. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions also rose from 51.3% in the second quarter to 54.3% in the fourth quarter, also well above the statutory minimum of 25%.  Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio 1. Consolidated position. 2. Quarterly average figures.  The Net Stable Funding Ratio, one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, indicates that the funding positions of authorized institutions are stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 135.6% in the fourth quarter of 2018 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.3%, also exceeding the statutory minimum of 50% applicable in 2018. The ample liquidity and sound funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks.  Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio  Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the banking system's maintenance of a stable funding structure. At end-2018, the proportion of Customer deposits in total liabilities of all authorized institutions rose slightly to 55.7% from 54.5% six months earlier (Chart 5.9). As total loans and advances declined during the second half of 2018 while total deposits increased over the same period, the loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions in all currencies fell from 75.7% at end-June 2018 to 72.6% at year-end (Chart 5.10). Similarly, the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions declined from 65.2% to 58.3% over the same period. In contrast, the HKD loan-to-deposit ratio edged up from 85.4% at end-June 2018 to 86.9% at year-end, as HKD deposit growth was significantly lower than HKD loan growth.  Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratios of all authorized institutions  The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks declined slightly in the second half of 2018. It is estimated that, under a shock of a 200 basis points across-the-board rise in interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 2.44% of their total capital base at end-2018 (Chart 5.11). Nonetheless, given the uncertain pace of further US rate increases, banks should closely monitor their interest rate risk management. Against a backdrop of continued uncertainty over the China-US trade conflict, tightening global financial liquidity, and slowing global economic growth, credit growth slowed significantly in the second half of 2018. However, credit growth has shown signs of stabilisation since November 2018. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions declined by 0.9% in the second half of 2018, following a 5.3% increase in the first half (Chart 5.12). This decline was due to a slowdown in local loans (including loans used in Hong Kong and trade finance) and a decrease in loans used outside Hong Kong. Local loan growth slowed to 0.1% in the second half of the year, while loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.0% over the same period, compared with growth of 5.3% and 5.2% respectively in the first half. For 2018 as a whole, the overall loan growth rate slowed significantly from 16.1% in 2017 to 4.4%.  Chart 5.12 Loan growth  Looking ahead, credit demand may remain weak in the near term. The Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook conducted by the HKMA in December 2018 showed that, among all authorized institutions surveyed, 82% expected loan demand to remain unchanged in the next three months, while the proportion expecting demand to decrease rose to 18% (Table 5.A).  Despite the slight decline in total loans in the second half of 2018, the asset quality of banks' loan portfolios remained sound. The gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions edged down slightly to 0.55% and 0.36% respectively at end-December 2018, compared with 0.61% and 0.40% at end-June 2018. For retail banks, the gross CLR decreased slightly to 0.50%, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans edged up slightly to 0.32% (Chart 5.13). Both ratios are low by historical standards. On a half-yearly basis, personal loan growth slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to a slowdown in private loans (including credit card advances and other personal loans), which offset the rapid growth in residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As nominal GDP in Hong Kong grew more slowly than personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak that began in early 2020 has hit both demand and supply simultaneously, posing challenges to the global economy that are different from previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March to contain the economic impact of the outbreak, financial markets remain volatile and global financing conditions have tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and local environment, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets have continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the stronger side, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable, and total deposits growing moderately, no significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. Growth in total loans picked up moderately in the first half of 2019 before slowing in the second half. The residential property market softened broadly from mid-2019, albeit with some fluctuations. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of coronavirus, future Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions and local social incidents. Given the continued rise in corporate leverage and household debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on asset quality of their loan portfolios under conditions where these risk factors may intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth had begun to show initial signs of stabilisation, supported by intensified policy-easing by major central banks, an easing of trade tensions between the US and China, and a reduction in the risk of a no-deal Brexit. However, since late January, the increasing number of coronavirus cases globally has raised market concerns and triggered significant volatility in global financial markets. In response to the evolving risks of the outbreak, several major central banks have cut interest rates significantly and expanded liquidity facilities, while some governments have introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, global financing conditions have tightened amid rising credit spreads and sharp falls in equity markets. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus outbreak will weigh on global economic activity, and the magnitude of the economic impact will depend on the severity and duration of the outbreak. In the medium term, tensions between the US and its major trading partners may re-escalate, and trade negotiations between the UK and the EU following Brexit may prove difficult. Weak global demand continued to weigh on economic growth in East Asia.¹ Exports from East Asia to major destinations including the US, European economies and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region recently reported growth in revenues, but it remains to be seen whether the technology cycle is broadly recovering. Financial markets responded positively to the Phase One trade deal between China and the US announced in December 2019, with the trade truce reducing some of the uncertainties in global trade. Nonetheless, East Asia will continue to face headwinds including weak firms' earnings and high private sector leverage ratio. Meanwhile, the coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies may come under further pressure amid a continued slowdown in growth. Travel restrictions imposed by a number of regional economies may adversely affect Asian tourism, particularly those economies that are more reliant on tourism services exports. Given the close integration of regional supply chains with Mainland China, manufacturing activity may also be affected by the outbreak. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to moderate in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade deal between China and the US will help to temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressures remain given the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 placed maintaining economic stability as a key priority for 2020, while also focusing on the control of financial risks. The latest market consensus forecasts indicate that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, the Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite such measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have experienced a decline in equity in recent years, seen as a sign of "private sector retreat". Feature 2 examines the drivers of changes in equity of Mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 data from listed corporates, and finds that private enterprises or smaller enterprises are not inherently more prone to downsizing or "retreat". While the study finds that negative earnings are the most significant driver, other factors, particularly structural ones, also warrant attention (see Feature 2 for details). Local economic activity contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real GDP declined for three consecutive quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy had entered a recession. As a result, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year of 2019, worse than the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018 and the first annual contraction since 2009. A slowdown in domestic demand, particularly a decline in private consumption, was the primary factor dragging down GDP growth in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activity, leading to a weakened economic outlook and dampening consumer and business sentiment. Hong Kong's external trade performance continued to be subdued amid renewed US-China trade frictions, a global economic slowdown, and a sharp decline in inbound tourism. In light of the significant headwinds facing the economy, the government introduced several rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To provide banks with more room to step up their support for the local economy and to help cushion the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, which would allow banks to release an additional lending capacity of HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion to businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the outbreak has recently introduced material downside risks. As sectors such as retail, accommodation services, food and beverage services, tourism and transportation have yet to recover from the disruption caused by social incidents, the outbreak will deal a double blow to these industries. However, the series of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget will provide relief to households and businesses, particularly SMEs, including a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and preferential low-interest loans with 100% government guarantee under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme for businesses.² The HKMA further lowered the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020, which will give banks more room to increase their support for the local economy, especially sectors and individuals facing greater near-term stress due to the outbreak. In terms of GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business sentiment. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the Phase One trade deal between China and the US is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the near term.³ However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to drag on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-border economic activities such as tourism, thereby limiting Hong Kong's export performance. The government forecasts real GDP growth in 2020 to be in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the average forecast by international institutions and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to a multitude of uncertainties and risks, including a global economic slowdown, US-China trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and local social incidents. The labour market came under greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment falling, the unemployment rate rising, and the real wage index declining on a year-on-year basis. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of social incidents and the coronavirus outbreak on the retail, accommodation and food services sectors. Looking ahead, the unemployment rate is expected to rise further given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak. Feature 3 examines recent developments in the labour market and its near-term outlook in greater detail. Local inflationary pressures continued to build up through the third quarter of 2019, driven mainly by rising fresh pork prices; inflation momentum subsequently moderated as economic activity weakened. Inflation is expected to ease in the near term due to weak economic conditions, consolidation in residential rentals, and moderate imported inflation. Market consensus forecasts for headline inflation in 2020 range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5%. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October 2019, supported by increased HKD demand related to equity activities, including IPOs. Upward momentum in the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened further in December, partly due to buoyant IPO activity and partly due to the unwinding of short HKD positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards year-end. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards end-February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period, without triggering any CUs. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term HKD interbank interest rates have been volatile, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Feature 4 examines how market attention to forthcoming IPO activities affects 3-month HIBORs. Meanwhile, the composite interest rate gradually rose from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020, reflecting banks' continued adjustments to preferential deposit rates to attract deposit funding. As some banks raised the interest rate caps set with reference to Best Lending Rates, the average lending rate on new mortgage loans rose to around 2.6% in October, but edged down to around 2.5% in January 2020 as Best Lending Rates in the market were lowered from November onwards. With the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the stronger side, the Aggregate Balance remaining stable, and total deposits growing moderately, no significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact of a further deterioration of the coronavirus outbreak amid external uncertainties. Hong Kong has substantial foreign reserves and a robust banking system, and the HKMA has the capability, resources and determination to handle capital outflows and to maintain monetary and financial stability in Hong Kong. During the review period, both CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates strengthened on market expectations of a US-China trade deal, but have faced weakening pressure since late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In the latter part of 2019, CNH traded at a broadly premium to the onshore renminbi, while the discount widened briefly at end-January 2020, though the spread remained modest by historical standards. Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool recovered slightly after a mild decline in the previous review period. As at end-January 2020, RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit balances increased to RMB637.4 billion. Other RMB businesses in Hong Kong also grew, with strong growth recorded in RMB bank loans and RMB trade settlements in Hong Kong. The daily average transaction volume of the RMB RTGS system maintained a high level of RMB1,133.9 billion for the full year of 2019. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of the Mainland capital account, increased allocation to RMB assets by international investors, and deepened regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives.

Towards end-2019, signs of stabilisation in global economic activity had raised market hopes for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the rising number of coronavirus cases worldwide has dashed recovery hopes, deepening investor concerns over a global recession and triggering sell-offs in global financial markets. To counter the economic impact, major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has clouded the outlook for economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to weigh on regional economic growth in the near term, with the tourism sector being particularly hard hit. Meanwhile, East Asian economies continue to face the challenges of weak corporate profitability and elevated private sector leverage ratio. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 amid weak domestic demand and external demand. Looking ahead, while the signing of the Phase One trade deal between China and the US helps to temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downward pressures remain in the face of the coronavirus outbreak, continued economic rebalancing and the impact of the global economic slowdown, though monetary and fiscal policy responses by the authorities will provide some buffer. Against the backdrop of persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainty, manufacturing and investment remained sluggish, and global economic growth remained subdued in the second half of 2019. However, growth showed preliminary signs of stabilisation in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), supported in part by earlier policy easing by the Fed and the ECB, as well as an easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the US-China "Phase One" trade deal. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index Since late January, however, the rising number of coronavirus cases worldwide and the ensuing economic disruptions have caused market concerns, triggering sell-offs in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major export destination globally and plays an important role in the global supply chain, disruptions to production activities on the Mainland and a drag on its economic growth would generate significant spillover effects with the potential to affect the rest of the world (Chart 2.3). Since late February, a surge in coronavirus cases outside Mainland China could exacerbate disruptions to the supply chain and pose risks of directly weighing on local economic activity.5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bonds Index Option-Adjusted Spread Chart 2.3 Exports of goods and services of selected major advanced economies to Mainland China in 2018 (as a percentage of their GDP) To counter the potentially severe economic impact of the epidemic, some central banks (including the Fed, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. Nonetheless, financial markets continue to face significant selling pressure, leading to a notable tightening of global financing conditions, which could in turn amplify global downward pressures on the economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index Beyond the development of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. In particular, regarding trade tensions, while policy risks have receded following the conclusion of the Phase One trade deal between China and the US, subsequent negotiations are likely to be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain to be resolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to go smoothly, prolonging post-Brexit uncertainties. In addition, the sharp decline in oil prices since March will put pressure on major oil-exporting emerging market economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained subdued in the second half of 2019 due to weak global demand. East Asian merchandise exports to major destinations including the US, European economies and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). While there are preliminary signs that the downcycle of regional electronics products is bottoming out, including reports by major regional electronics companies of improved profitability in late 2019,6 it remains to be seen whether a meaningful rebound in regional electronics exports has taken hold. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise exports to major destinations Persistently sluggish economic growth and trade uncertainties have also weighed on investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation declining in most East Asian economies in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which could affect the region's potential economic growth over the longer term. To support growth in an environment of moderate inflation, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines and South Korea cut their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after having lowered them in the first half of the year, while the Bank of Thailand also cut its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross fixed capital formation The coronavirus outbreak has raised concerns that regional economies could come under further pressure on top of persistently weak growth. As many regional economies have imposed travel restrictions vis-à-vis Mainland China, the tourism sector has been the most hard-hit, in particular those economies that are more reliant on tourists from Mainland China and tourism services exports (Chart 2.7). A prolonged and intensified epidemic would also affect regional supply chains that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism exports and Chinese visitors In the near term, the epidemic will continue to affect economic activity and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the SARS outbreak in 2003, these effects could be short-lived, but the actual outcome will depend on the severity and spread of the epidemic as well as the effectiveness of government actions to contain it. At the same time, East Asian economies face multiple headwinds. First, despite market expectations of a near-term deterioration in corporate profitability (Chart 2.8), loose global monetary conditions have encouraged yield-seeking activities, driving up asset prices beyond what fundamentals would justify. As a result, regional equity markets are more susceptible to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Consensus earnings forecasts for benchmark equity index constituents Second, weak corporate profitability and economic growth could make it harder for private sector entities in the region to service their debts. While lower domestic interest rates can provide some breathing room for indebted companies and households, they could also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Moreover, as discussed in Feature 1, the risk of private sector debt overhang could also be exacerbated as more index-driven funds flow into regional financial markets, though such effects may be confined to companies with sounder financial fundamentals and their longer-term borrowings. Third, on the external front, East Asian economies may also face heightened risks from increasingly protectionist US trade policy. Despite recent progress on the Phase One trade deal between China and the US, US-China trade tensions persist as fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain unresolved. As evidenced by the widening net trade surpluses of a number of regional economies vis-à-vis the US (Chart 2.9), multinational corporations may continue to diversify their sourcing beyond China-centric supply chains to avoid tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative net trade surplus of nine Asian emerging market economies (excluding China) with the US had risen to around US$167 billion. If net trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, the Asian economies concerned could become the next targets in trade conflicts; for instance, the US government imposed hefty tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019.7 Against this backdrop, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain despite the US-China trade truce. Chart 2.9 Merchandise net trade surpluses with the US Over the past decade, the intensification of international financial market integration has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that as much as 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds.8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly referred to as passive funds), but also actively managed funds that benchmark against investment indices.9 By introducing overseas investors that the relevant economies might otherwise be unable to attract or reach, these funds help to foster the development of financial markets in emerging market economies. As such, these funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, contributing to the long-term growth and stability of their markets. But is there really a free lunch? With respect to passive bond funds, there are market concerns that investments by such funds could undermine the financial discipline of the corporate bonds issuers in which they invest, thereby contributing to elevated corporate leverage.10 In addition, some argue that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has amplified the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, rendering emerging market economies, which are already highly sensitive to global factors and subject to other common influences, even more vulnerable.11 This Feature assesses the implications of index-driven investment for financial stability with respect to these two propositions. In accordance with the weights of constituent bonds in a benchmark index, passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to the relevant bonds. Consequently, compared with actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may reduce the incentive of the corporate bonds issuers to act in the interest of fund investors.13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behaviour could encourage overborrowing, posing significant credit and debt repayment abilities risks to the corporate sector of emerging market economies, which has seen a sharp rise in leverage ratio since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate leverage in emerging market economies Using the weights of corporates in emerging market economies within a mainstream index tracking corporate bonds of emerging market economies as a proxy for their bonds' exposure to passive bond fund investments,14 we find that an increase in such investment raises the long-term (but not short-term) leverage ratio of the corporate bond issuers concerned. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 show the estimated effects. Apart from promoting the development of the corporate bond market in emerging market economies, the expanded long-term bond investor base facilitated by passive bond funds also benefits corporates in emerging market economies. We also find that the above effects are only significant for corporates in emerging market economies with sounder fundamentals (in particular, those with stronger debt repayment abilities and lower leverage ratio) (solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Faced with higher financial distress costs, highly leveraged corporates or those with weaker debt repayment abilities appear not to be further drawn into a debt trap by passive bond fund investments. In sum, the above analysis suggests that the growth in passive bond fund investment need not significantly increase debt repayment abilities risks in the corporate sector of emerging market economies.

Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019 due to weakening private consumption, declining investment spending, and poor export performance, entering its first recession since 2009. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, with the coronavirus outbreak recently introducing significant downside risks. The economic outlook is being shaped by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the slowdown in global economic growth, the state of Sino-US trade tensions, economic performance in Mainland China, and developments in local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate is likely to rise further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to moderate, though the outlook is subject to both upside and downside risks.  Hong Kong's economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real GDP contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the contraction in the second half, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the full year, worse than the 2.9% growth recorded in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since the global financial crisis in 2009.  Figure 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions from major expenditure components  On a quarter-on-quarter basis, economic activity slowed markedly in the second half (Figure 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. On the domestic front, private consumption was the primary drag on GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely disrupted consumption activity, which in turn weakened the economic outlook and dampened consumer confidence, causing private consumption to contract sharply from the third quarter onwards.33 Total investment spending remained weak due to heightened economic uncertainty and deteriorating business sentiment, dragging down fourth-quarter GDP.34  On the external front, Hong Kong's external trade performance continued to be subdued amid escalating Sino-US trade tensions, weakening global economic growth, and a sharp decline in visitor arrivals (Figure 3.2).35 Net exports weighed on GDP in the third quarter under the impact of a sharp contraction in service exports, but supported GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance.  Figure 3.2 Real imports and exports  In light of the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government introduced multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to relieve the financial burden on citizens, safeguard employment, and support businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and severely affected sectors such as retail, food and beverage services, transport, and tourism.36 To provide banks with greater room to step up support for the local economy and help smooth the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on 14 October a reduction in the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, enabling banks to release an additional lending capacity of HKD 200 to 300 billion for businesses, including SMEs.  Economic performance in Hong Kong in 2020 is expected to face considerable challenges, with the epidemic recently introducing significant downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruption caused by the social incidents, the epidemic will deliver a double blow to these industries. Nevertheless, the package of counter-cyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and businesses, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), including a one-off cash payment to adult permanent residents and concessionary low-interest loans with 100% government guarantees under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme for businesses.37 The HKMA's further reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on 16 March 2020 will provide banks with greater capacity to step up support for the local economy, especially for those sectors and individuals facing greater short-term pressure due to the epidemic.  Looking at GDP components, private consumption and investment spending are likely to remain weak given fragile consumer and business sentiment. While government consumption will support economic growth, public investment spending is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects near completion. On the external front, the Phase One trade deal between the US and China is expected to have a modest positive impact on the local economy in the near term.38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activity will continue to weigh on Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak could disrupt regional supply chains and slow cross-boundary economic activities such as tourism, thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance.  The Government forecasts real GDP growth in 2020 to be in the range of -1.5% to 0.5%, while the average of market consensus forecasts from international and private sector analysts stands at -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is shaped by the numerous uncertainties and risks discussed in preceding chapters.  The labour market faced increasing pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Figure 3.3). Among sectors, the unemployment rate in retail, accommodation, and food and beverage services surged to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe damage caused by the social incidents.39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was driven mainly by the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food and beverage services, and construction sectors. Real wages also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter.  Looking ahead, in light of the weak economic outlook described above, the labour market will continue to face mounting challenges, and the unemployment rate is likely to rise further. Feature 3 will examine recent developments and the near-term outlook of the labour market in greater detail.  Figure 3.3 Labour market conditions  Local inflationary pressures continued to build into the third quarter of 2019, driven mainly by rising fresh pork prices, before gradually easing as economic activity slowed. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying composite consumer price index rose by 3.3% in the third quarter, with the rate of increase easing slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The annualised three-month-on-three-month rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, also softened from a peak of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The moderation in inflation momentum reflected diminishing price pressures across a number of consumer price index components. On traded goods, food inflation remained notable on account of rising fresh pork prices, though price pressures for consumer goods such as clothing and footwear as well as durable goods remained mild. On services, the growth in the consumer price index rental component trended downward as the pace of increase in newly signed private residential rentals slowed (Figure 3.5). Labour cost pressures edged up somewhat but remained moderate in recent quarters (Figure 3.6).  Figure 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation Figure 3.5 Composite CPI rental component and market rentals Figure 3.6 Unit labour cost  Local inflationary pressures are expected to moderate in the near term. On the domestic front, weak economic conditions and a widening negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressures on local inflation. The housing rental component of inflation should moderate further as the slowdown in private residential rentals persists. On the external front, import inflation is expected to remain mild given weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts for headline inflation in 2020 range from 0.6% to 3.7%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation at 2.5% and headline inflation at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in the economy (for instance, if the coronavirus epidemic is prolonged) could further dampen inflation. On the other hand, a more severe disruption to the supply of fresh pork would exert upward pressure on inflation.  Despite the marked slowdown in the economy, the unemployment rate remained low at 2.8–2.9% during the first nine months of 2019. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate rose more noticeably to 3.3% by end-2019. The labour market will face greater headwinds in 2020 due to the impact of the coronavirus epidemic. Against this backdrop, this feature analyses recent developments and the near-term outlook of the labour market, including an examination of why the overall labour market remained broadly resilient (with little change in the unemployment rate) in the first three quarters of 2019, and what this implies for future developments. This feature also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate.  It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labour demand entails costs. In fact, the unemployment rate tends to lag the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by approximately two to three quarters (Figure B3.1). This lagging nature helps explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activity deteriorated sharply in the third quarter.  Figure B3.1 Real GDP growth and unemployment rate  On the labour demand side, while the escalation of Sino-US trade tensions and local social incidents inflicted heavy blows on employment in the trade and retail and tourism-related sectors respectively, a number of key sectors continued to underpin the overall labour market. Specifically, employment in the finance, business, public administration, social, and personal services sectors maintained growth in 2019, partially offsetting the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Figure B3.2). Despite the economic recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained robust, and financial activities related to fintech development and initial public offerings were very active. These factors may have helped support employment in the financial and business services sectors. Furthermore, the public administration, social, and personal services sector, which encompasses education, healthcare, and social work activities, appears to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation coefficients analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the public administration, social, and personal services sector responds more neutrally to the economic cycle. In other words, even during an economic slowdown, employment in these sectors may not be significantly affected by cyclical fluctuations.  Figure B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019  On the labour supply side, the labour force participation rate40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Figure B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate (blue line). As illustrated, the labour force participation rate (green bar) exerted downward pressures on the unemployment rate in 2019.41 On the other hand, the increase in total employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bar) also helped contain the unemployment rate. However, as the economy contracted sharply in the second half, the decline in employment exerted upward pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, while total employment fell during the recession, the lower labour force participation rate helped alleviate the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019.  Figure B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate  Some structural changes in the labour market also merit attention. In particular, the growing proportion of voluntary part-time employees may have helped companies retain workers. Indeed, while the shares of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment have declined to around 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second largest group within the total employed population (around 7% in 2017).42 As a result, companies may be able to retain or hire more workers by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that the average weekly working hours have declined, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to approximately 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the greater proportion of part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened from October onwards, with the upward momentum gathering further pace in December, keeping the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range for the past few months. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was partly driven by equity-related demand, and partly by the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions as liquidity tightened towards the year-end. Overall, Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to function in a smooth and orderly manner. Although fund flow volatility may increase amid uncertain external conditions as the coronavirus outbreak weighs on market sentiment, Hong Kong's ample foreign reserves and robust banking system provide the capacity to withstand fund outflow pressures without affecting the city's financial stability.  Supported by increased equity-related Hong Kong dollar demand (including IPO-related flows), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate gradually strengthened from mid-October (Chart 4.1). As December arrived, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar intensified further, with the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remaining on the strong side of the Convertibility Undertaking range from mid-December through February. The strengthening of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate was partly attributable to buoyant IPO activity, and partly to the unwinding of Hong Kong dollar short positions as liquidity tightened towards the year-end. After the Lunar New Year holiday, funding positions eased and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on 28 February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to function in a smooth and orderly manner during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side CUs were triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance of the banking system remained largely unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Hong Kong Dollar Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes  The Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index broadly tracked movements in the US dollar, edging up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was minimal, the impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index was limited, and its movement broadly followed that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates  When assessing fund flows in Hong Kong, it is essential to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts: (1) Hong Kong dollar fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. Hong Kong dollar fund flows focus on the monetary dimension of fund flows and are useful for assessing monetary stability, particularly under the LERS. Cross-border fund flows, on the other hand, focus on the geographical movement of funds through Hong Kong's banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. The two concepts require different monitoring indicators.  When monitoring Hong Kong dollar fund flows, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance of the banking system warrant close attention. If the public or investors convert their Hong Kong dollar assets into foreign currency assets in large quantities, demand for Hong Kong dollars will naturally decline, causing the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate to weaken. Under the LERS, if the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate weakens to the 7.85 weak-side CU level, the HKMA stands ready to buy Hong Kong dollars from banks on request, resulting in a decline in the Aggregate Balance of the banking system. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has remained broadly stable, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has been on the strong side of the CUs range in recent months, so no significant outflow from the Hong Kong dollar was observed during the review period.  Total bank deposits in Hong Kong serve as a useful indicator for monitoring cross-border fund flows. When there is a significant fund outflow from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will necessarily decline. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating no significant cross-border fund outflow.  Hong Kong's foreign exchange and money markets continued to function in a smooth and orderly manner, suggesting that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on the local monetary environment has remained limited thus far. Nevertheless, risks arising from the coronavirus outbreak warrant close monitoring. With ample foreign reserves and a robust banking system, the HKMA has the capability, resources and determination to address fund outflow and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability.  Despite uncertain external conditions and a slowdown in the local economy, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The HKD Monetary Base remained sizeable, rising 4.0% since end-June to HK$1,689.4 billion at end-January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As no CUs were triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance of the banking system remained largely unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the monetary base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued notes and coins in circulation, rose steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base  During the review period, broad Hong Kong dollar monetary aggregates remained broadly stable. Hong Kong dollar broad money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, before edging up by 0.2% over the seven months from end-June 2019. Counterpart analysis shows that the growth in HKD M3 since end-June mainly reflected increases in banks' net foreign currency assets and a rise in the monetary base (driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued notes and coins in circulation) (Chart 4.5). Over the seven months since end-June, Hong Kong dollar deposits (the major component of HKD M3) remained broadly stable (Chart 4.6). Within Hong Kong dollar deposits, time deposits continued to grow at a moderate pace, partly reflecting higher Hong Kong dollar deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in HKD M3 and Counterparts  Over the seven months since end-June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), driven mainly by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during the period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% over the same period, with renminbi deposits recording a slight decline in Hong Kong dollar terms. Overall, total deposits of AIs grew steadily by 1.2% since end-June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since end-June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may be subject to volatility caused by various short-term factors — such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities — the figures should be interpreted with care. Chart 4.6 Deposits of AIs by Currency Chart 4.7 Total Broad Money Supply (M2)  Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term HKD interbank interest rates exhibited volatility reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital markets activity since Q4 2019. In particular, buoyant IPO activity in the Hong Kong stock market caused the Hong Kong dollar overnight HIBORs to fluctuate more widely in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8).44 During the review period, other short-term HIBORs generally rose. Large new stock listings exerted significant upward pressure on overnight HIBORs, and a thematic box using empirical analysis (Feature 4) shows that market participants' attention to upcoming IPO activity also influences the 3-month HIBORs. This occurs when market participants anticipate the future subscription deadlines of large new listings in advance and prepare medium-term HKD funds ahead of time. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD Interbank Interest Rates  Regarding the Hong Kong dollar yield curve, it shifted downward in tandem with the US dollar yield curve. Compared with end-June 2019, the 10-year Hong Kong Government bond yields fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% as of 28 February 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, 3-year Hong Kong Government bond yields declined by 50 basis points over the same period to 1.00%. Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate and Average Lending Rate on New Mortgage Loans  At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds of retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at end-July 2019 to 1.01% at end-January 2020. This increase mainly reflected banks continuing to raise their preferential deposit rates to attract deposits, resulting in a rise in the Hong Kong dollar weighted deposit rate. Following the reduction in the US federal funds rate target range in late October 2019, several retail banks lowered their Best Lending Rates by 12.5 basis points. As a result, the Best Lending Rates of retail banks currently stand in the range of 5.00% to 5.50%.  Regarding mortgage lending, for HIBOR-based mortgage loans, major banks raised the interest rate cap pegged to the Best Lending Rate, causing the average lending rate on new mortgage loans to rise to around 2.63% in October.45 Following the reduction in Best Lending Rates in the market since November, the average lending rate on mortgage loans edged down slightly to 2.53% in January 2020.  In response to evolving risks to US economic activity posed by the coronavirus outbreak and to support the Federal Reserve in meeting its policy goals, the Fed reduced the target range for the federal funds rate by a cumulative 150 basis points to 0–0.25% on 3 March (US time) and 15 March (US time). While HIBORs broadly track their USD counterparts over the longer term, short-term HKD interbank interest rates may be influenced by local factors that affect demand for Hong Kong dollars, such as the local IPO activity. As the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has declined since April 2018, HIBORs may have become more sensitive to changes in the supply and demand for HKD funds. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet interbank payment and settlement needs. In fact, the Hong Kong interbank market has continued to function in an orderly manner. Should liquidity tighten in the short term, banks may make use of the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA.  Against the backdrop of potentially escalating China-US trade conflict, the CNH and onshore renminbi exchange rates depreciated significantly in late August and September 2019, with the CNH falling to a ten-year low of 7.19 against the US dollar on 2 September (Chart 4.10). As market expectations of a resumption of China-US trade negotiations emerged in October, the depreciation trend reversed, with both the CNH and onshore renminbi strengthening in Q4, and briefly breaking above the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020 following the signing of the Phase One trade deal between China and the US. However, since late January, both the CNH and onshore renminbi have come under renewed depreciation pressure amid the coronavirus outbreak. The CNH traded at a discount to the onshore renminbi for most of the period from May to August, and broadly at a premium in the latter part of 2019, while the discount widened briefly at end-January 2020, though the spread remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates  Despite volatility in the renminbi exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the 3-month CNH HIBOR continued to hover in the range of 3–4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief bouts of volatility in late August and late November due to Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI)'s A-share rebalancing, and again in late January 2020 as the Lunar New Year holiday approached.

The profitability of Hong Kong retail banks recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019 amid increasing uncertainties in both the global and local economic environments. Nonetheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and sound by international standards. Asset quality remained healthy by historical standards. While growth in total loans slowed in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the period under review. Correspondingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratios for all currencies and Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratios of all AIs both rose. Nevertheless, the liquidity conditions of the banking sector remained sound, given that the aggregate balance of the banking system stayed at a stable level and deposits remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face a number of downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future trajectory of Sino-US trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. In light of the continued rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. In the second half of 2019, overall pre-tax operating profit59 of retail banks fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, compared with 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), retail banks' net interest income continued to record moderate growth during the period under review. However, loan impairment charges and operating expenses of retail banks both increased, leading to a slight decline in profitability. Chart 5.1 Retail bank profitability Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Despite the Fed Funds target rate being cut three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, there have been no significant downward pressures in the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market so far. On the contrary, short-tenor HKD interbank interest rates have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019, driven by a number of local factors including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand from large IPOs, and tighter interbank market liquidity conditions. Meanwhile, longer-tenor HKD interbank interest rates remained broadly stable during the period under review, with the three-month HIBORs standing at 2.43% at end-2019, close to the level six months earlier (blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, there was limited room for retail banks to follow the US policy rate cuts given that Hong Kong dollar savings deposits rates remained close to zero.60 On the other hand, banks continued to compete for longer-term stable deposit funding as HKD liquidity in the banking system tightened during the period under review.61 Reflecting an increase in the weighted cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average cost of HKD funds of retail banks) gradually rose from 0.95% six months ago to 1.09% at end-2019, though it remained at a low level by historical standards (green line in Chart 5.3). Chart 5.3 Interest rates Taking a broader perspective, the average overall cost of HKD funds and USD counterparts of locally incorporated licensed banks edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019, as the decline in USD funding costs of locally incorporated licensed banks more than offset the slight increase in their HKD funding costs (Chart 5.4). During the period under review, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decrease in their overall cost of funding and the relatively high level of HKD interbank interest rates, providing support to banking sector profitability during the same period. Chart 5.4 Cost of HKD funds and USD counterparts and tenor of licensed banks 1. Starting from June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book framework will submit returns under the new framework, while exempt licensed banks will continue to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall cost of funding and tenor have been calculated as the weighted average of the relevant figures for both types of licensed banks. Accordingly, figures from June 2019 onwards are not directly comparable with those for previous months. Looking ahead, a number of external and local environmental downside risks will continue to cast a shadow over banks' earnings outlook. These include uncertainties from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of Sino-US trade relations, and the intensification of geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors could dampen already-weak global economic growth momentum and reduce credit demand for bank lending. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the low global interest rate environment could persist, which may put pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to weigh on business investment and market confidence. Against a backdrop of already-weak economic conditions, if the situation continues or worsens in the future, the outlook for credit demand and bank asset quality could deteriorate. In terms of overall market developments, the Hong Kong banking sector has started launching virtual banking services following the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's granting of eight virtual banking licences. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by offering more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this could put upward pressure on the cost of funding of incumbent banks. While the near-term impact may be moderate given the currently limited scale of virtual banks' operations, the longer-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks accelerate their adoption of financial technology to remain competitive. The results of Feature 5 show that the degree of fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically correlated with improvements in cost efficiency and profitability levels. The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained sound and well above the minimum international standards. At end-2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions further increased to 20.7% (Chart 5.5).
