The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines has brought hopes of economic reopening, boosting the global growth outlook. Combined with continued fiscal and monetary policy-easing measures, financial markets have repeatedly reached new highs. Nevertheless, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery is expected to vary across economies. In the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, elevated debt levels, and the lasting economic scars inflicted by the pandemic will pose challenges for policymakers going forward. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, driven mainly by equity-related demand. During the period under review, total deposits increased, with no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Reflecting in part the weakness in economic activity and subdued credit demand due to recurring waves of the pandemic, total lending in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, though it still recorded a marginal increase for the full year 2020. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties over the pace of economic recovery and continued geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges for the Hong Kong banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic could weaken the repayment ability of businesses and households, the banking sector should remain vigilant about the impact of these downside risks on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as economies reopened, but renewed rises in COVID-19 infection numbers from the fourth quarter caused global growth to slow again. Nonetheless, with vaccine development achieving a breakthrough at the end of 2020, markets anticipated that the pandemic would eventually come to an end, which would facilitate a return to normalcy and an acceleration of global economic growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary policy-easing measures, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, even as signs of disconnect from the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to overshadow the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. At the same time, supply bottlenecks and the earlier aggressive easing measures could lead to inflation exceeding expectations, which in turn could prompt central banks to reduce monetary easing earlier than anticipated, ending financial markets' expectations of a "lower for longer" monetary policy. In the longer term, policymakers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the many economic legacies of the pandemic, including elevated global debt levels and lasting economic scarring. In East Asia, real GDP growth in the second half of 2020 improved, supported by a recovery in export demand. With increased risk appetite, portfolio investment inflows into the region rebounded, and yield-seeking activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, the East Asian region still faces persistent uncertainties stemming from the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less-developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, impeding the recovery of their tourism and services sectors. Second, potential variability in vaccine supply, coverage, or efficacy, coupled with the weakened fiscal positions of regional governments, could dampen market sentiment and trigger reversals in capital flows. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020 as consumption activities gradually returned to normal. For the full year 2020, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive GDP growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook will remain largely dependent on the development of the pandemic and the evolution of Sino-US tensions. The latest market consensus forecasts suggest that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The renminbi depreciated for several months at the beginning of 2020, before strengthening for the remainder of the year as economic recovery gathered pace, the US dollar weakened, and strong capital inflows were recorded in the Mainland bond market. A detailed study revealed that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamental factors, rather than market sentiment, played a more important role in driving renminbi exchange rate movements (see Feature 1 for details). Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level. Seasonally adjusted real GDP began to recover in the third quarter, driven by a moderate increase in domestic demand and further expansion in exports of goods, ending five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction in real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to approximately 3% in the second half. For the full year 2020, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and the first instance in history of two consecutive years of contraction, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry indicate that consumption and tourism-related sectors contracted more sharply than the overall economy under the pandemic. In response to the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two additional rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to assist industries and members of the public affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recently released 2021/22 Budget to stimulate the economy, including the disbursement of one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and a 100% government-guaranteed personal loan scheme for unemployed individuals. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, along with an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. With COVID-19 vaccines offering hopes of a return to normalcy in economic activity, the local economy is expected to return to positive growth for the full year 2021, although the strength and pace of recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including pandemic developments and the progress and effectiveness of vaccine rollout. Given that the widespread administration of vaccines will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% in 2021, while the average growth forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts stands at 4.4%. Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and in early 2021. The unemployment rate rose further, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate climbed to 4.0%, the highest level since the SARS epidemic. In response to the continued deterioration in labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced further targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide additional support to sectors hardest hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure amid weak economic conditions. Feature 2 examines the potential impact of fluctuations in inbound tourism on the local labour market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease over the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. Underlying consumer price inflation fell significantly on a year-on-year basis to 0.3% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and declined further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. Underlying inflation measured on a three-month annualised basis, which reflects inflation momentum, remained at subdued levels in recent months, albeit with slight fluctuations. Given that global and local economic conditions remain challenging, inflationary pressures in Hong Kong are likely to remain mild in the near term, particularly as the slowdown in newly signed private residential rental growth will continue to weigh on local inflation. Market consensus forecasts point to a moderate headline inflation rate of 1.4% for 2021, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation and headline inflation of 1.0% and 1.6% respectively for 2021. The Hong Kong dollar traded close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, driven mainly by equity-related funding demand, including that from buoyant IPO fund-raising activities and southbound capital inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect schemes. IPO fund-raising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar on the strong side. During the period under review, the strong-side CUs were triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, resulting in HK$263.3 billion flowing into Hong Kong. For the full year 2020, the strong-side CUs were triggered a total of 85 times, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. From a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the period under review, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to pandemic developments, the pace of economic recovery, and continued Sino-US tensions may exacerbate fund flow volatility, Hong Kong's ample foreign reserves and robust banking system provide the capacity to withstand such volatility. As the triggering of the strong-side CUs led to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, HKD interbank interest rates generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, declined further from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.23% at end-February 2021. With lower funding costs, the average lending rate on new mortgage loans also fell from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the period under review, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. As the onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rate strengthened, the offshore CNH has appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the period under review, the CNH traded at a premium relative to the CNY, with the average premium in the fourth quarter standing at approximately 100 pips, which remains modest by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore renminbi liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit outstanding increasing to RMB826.3 billion as of end-January 2021. As for other renminbi business activities, RMB bank loans in Hong Kong decreased, while RMB trade settlements grew, and the average daily transaction volume of the RMB RTGS system remained elevated at RMB1,191.5 billion throughout 2020. With Hong Kong's efficient financial infrastructure providing investors with a wide range of cross-border capital flow channels connecting the Mainland, the city's offshore renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continued opening of the Mainland capital account, increasing international investor demand for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative. Supported by the rise in global equity markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors through Stock Connect, the local stock market rebounded after a sharp decline at the beginning of the period under review. Global equity markets rose, driven by unprecedented monetary policy-easing measures adopted by major economies, market optimism over positive progress in vaccine development which was seen as potentially facilitating a faster recovery in economic activity, and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recouped its losses following a steep decline in 2020, rising 15.1% during the period under review and briefly breaking through the 31,000-point level in mid-February 2021, reaching a 32-month high. Supported by steady issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and CNH debt market continued to expand in the second half of 2020. After experiencing significant net capital outflows in the first half of 2020, bond fund inflows into the local market rebounded swiftly as confidence was restored following the announcement of unprecedented economic stimulus measures by governments around the world. Despite a moderate rebound in bond yields during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, continued to hover near historically low levels.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, markets expected the COVID-19 pandemic to eventually come to an end, enabling the global economy to accelerate its growth going forward. Coupled with expectations of a "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors were undeterred by the resurgence of the pandemic at the end of 2020, and financial markets rose to new highs at the start of 2021. However, the buoyant expectations in financial markets were at odds with the still challenging macroeconomic environment, and should the pace of economic recovery fall short of expectations, or policy support be withdrawn earlier than anticipated (for instance due to inflation exceeding expectations), asset prices could become volatile. Looking ahead, policymakers face the challenge of deciding when to withdraw support measures and addressing the many issues left in the wake of the pandemic, including elevated debt levels and lasting economic scarring. The continued uncertainty surrounding the pandemic continues to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in East Asia, and less developed emerging market economies in the region may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in the rollout of vaccination programmes could reverse current optimism and destabilise capital flows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, the pace of economic recovery picked up in the second half of 2020 as consumption activity gradually returned to normal. Looking ahead, the economic outlook remains highly uncertain, largely dependent on how the pandemic evolves and how Sino-US tensions develop. In response, the government announced that it would maintain a supportive policy stance, while emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks. Buoyed by the purchasing power unleashed by economic reopening, major economies largely recorded better-than-expected real GDP growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, COVID-19 infection numbers surged again, prompting governments to reinstate lockdowns and social distancing measures, and global growth momentum weakened once more. Towards the end of 2020, more transmissible variants of the virus emerged and subsequently spread around the world, further complicating the situation. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and multiple vaccines receiving regulatory approval at the end of 2020, markets expected the pandemic to eventually end and the global economy to return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery came from continued policy stimulus measures, including commitments by major central banks to a "lower for longer" monetary policy against a backdrop of subdued inflation, as well as continued fiscal policy easing in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund revised upward its 2021 global real GDP growth forecast to 5.5% in January 2021, 0.3 percentage points higher than its October 2020 projection (Figure 2.1). Figure 2.1: International Monetary Fund real GDP growth forecasts made in January 2021 and October 2020. Against this backdrop, market sentiment improved, stock prices in cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery rose, driving global equity prices and valuations to new highs at the start of 2021 (Figure 2.2). Figure 2.2: 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major equity indices. However, while financial markets have performed strongly, the macroeconomic environment remains challenging, and the disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets amid multiple risks. First, the prospects for pandemic containment hinge on the broad distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Figure 2.3). Although global mechanisms such as COVAX exist to facilitate more equitable vaccine distribution, the low vaccination rate among lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more acute given limited vaccine supply. If pandemic control falls short of expectations, regions may need to extend social distancing measures and other restrictive measures, thereby weighing on global recovery prospects. Figure 2.3: Share of the population having received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021). Second, the rebound in financial markets is predicated on continued monetary and fiscal policy support, particularly the "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures could be withdrawn sooner than expected. For example, inflation expectations in the United States and Europe have risen amid supply bottlenecks, strong monetary and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal policy easing (Figure 2.4). Should inflation prove stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back policy-easing, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also cause financial markets to become more volatile. Figure 2.4: US and Euro area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates. Third, there is significant uncertainty over the future trajectory of Sino-US relations. The trend of Sino-US "decoupling", particularly in the financial and technology sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly hawkish stance towards Mainland China among both Republican and Democratic parties in the United States, this trend may not reverse under the Biden administration. An unexpected escalation in Sino-US tensions could trigger turmoil in financial markets in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to grapple with the question of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While withdrawing such measures too early could jeopardise the economic recovery and cause a "cliff effect", these measures are costly in the long run, including the fiscal burden they impose, and the delays they cause to the necessary post-pandemic reallocation of resources, such as allowing "zombie enterprises" whose business models are no longer viable to survive with continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many issues left behind by the pandemic. First, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 due to declining corporate revenues and surging government expenditure (Figure 2.5). While the sharp rise in debt may not pose an imminent problem given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, continued debt accumulation in both the public and private sectors could raise concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Figure 2.5: Global debt as a percentage of GDP. Another lingering issue involves the potential long-term economic losses or lasting scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, elevated uncertainty may reduce business investment, while workers who have been unemployed for extended periods may permanently exit the labour market, resulting in a significant waste of human capital. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilised in the second half of 2020 after a sharp contraction in the second quarter (Figure 2.6). The main driver of recovery came from a rebound in exports, with demand for electronics and technology equipment being particularly robust. At the same time, the most severely affected service sectors, such as tourism and consumer services requiring face-to-face interaction, continued to struggle. Figure 2.6: East Asia: real GDP growth in 2020. Despite continued uncertainty surrounding the recovery, portfolio investment flows have resumed. Since the second half of last year, the region attracted greater bond capital inflows driven by improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to bonds from advanced economies (Figure 2.7). As signs of economic recovery emerged and vaccine production plans were unveiled, equity capital inflows to East Asia also accelerated in the final quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated in line with portfolio inflows, with the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index rebounding by approximately 10% from its low in March of last year. Figure 2.7: East Asia: portfolio investment flows. East Asia continues to face the ongoing uncertainty posed by the pandemic. First, while the rollout of vaccines brings hope to the region's hard-hit service sectors and economy, competition among countries for early batches of vaccines has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacity. As a result, less developed economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination rates across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, as investor optimism is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or efficacy of vaccination falls significantly short of expectations, the current capital inflows and financial asset price rebound could come to an end. A sudden reversal of capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turbulence. As COVID-19 was brought under control and consumption gradually recovered, Mainland China's economy rebounded rapidly in the second half of 2020. At the same time, exports continued to grow, supported by strong demand for pandemic-related products such as medical devices and high-tech products (Figure 2.8). Over the course of 2020 as a whole, despite the unprecedented shock from the COVID-19 pandemic, Mainland China's GDP still recorded growth of 2.3%. Figure 2.8: Mainland China: contributions of demand components to GDP growth. Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts point to strong GDP growth of 8.4% for Mainland China in 2021, with private consumption expected to be the primary driver of economic growth. However, the sustainability of the recovery still depends to some extent on how the pandemic evolves. Although industrial production activity in Mainland China has normalised, the service sector continues to be partially disrupted as several northern provinces experienced fresh outbreaks. On the external front, while exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain as most developed economies grapple with new waves of the pandemic. Furthermore, Sino-US tensions may not ease in the near term, although the recently signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the concluded Comprehensive Agreement on Investment between China and the European Union could facilitate further integration between China and other economies, potentially partially offsetting the adverse effects of Sino-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Taking into account the continued uncertainty in the economic outlook, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that existing policy stances would not change significantly in 2021 to support economic growth, while also emphasising the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining stable macro leverage and debt sustainability of local government debt. In addition, the latest government work report set the growth target for 2021 at above 6%. In the longer term, the 14th Five-Year Plan has identified technological self-reliance and the dual circulation strategy as priority development directions, with the aim of achieving per capita GDP at the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on the repayment ability of bond issuers appears to have been limited, and the overall default rate in Mainland China's bond market remained low in the second half of 2020. However, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 due to a significant rise in defaults on state-owned enterprise bonds (Figure 2.9). While the increase in state-owned enterprise defaults primarily reflects the Central Government's determination to break the "implicit guarantee" on state-owned enterprise bonds in order to promote more rational market risk pricing, constrained fiscal space for some local governments — particularly those in less developed regions — may also have been a contributing factor. Figure 2.9: Mainland China: size and proportion of onshore bond defaults. In the second half of 2020, the cost of funding increased for corporate issuers, particularly for higher-risk issuers. Although continued economic recovery and the gradual normalisation of interest rates contributed to some extent to the rise in funding costs for lower-rated issuers, several corporate default events in the final quarter of 2020 led to a significant widening of interest rate differentials (Figure 2.10). Figure 2.10: Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields. In the housing market, property prices in Mainland China continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in first-tier cities. By contrast, property prices in lower-tier cities rose at a much slower pace (Figure 2.11). The housing oversupply problem that had plagued third-tier cities in previous years was largely brought under control in 2020, partly due to strong sales recorded by third-tier cities amid buoyant market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in third-tier cities stood at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months reached at the beginning of 2015.

Although real GDP remained well below its pre-pandemic level, Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020, supported by a recovery in domestic demand and further expansion in exports of goods. With the prospect of COVID-19 vaccination restoring normal economic activity, Hong Kong's economy is expected to return to growth in 2021 after recording its worst contraction on record in 2020. Nevertheless, the strength and pace of economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the pace and efficacy of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, Hong Kong's economy will continue to face significant challenges in early 2021. Consequently, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflationary pressures should stay mild.  Hong Kong's economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), though economic activity remained well below its pre-pandemic level. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. For 2020 as a whole, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and also the first time in history that two consecutive years of contraction were recorded, following a decline of 1.2% in 2019. The latest GDP data by industry also show that economic activity in the vast majority of sectors recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracting more sharply than the overall economy. On a quarter-on-quarter basis, real GDP began to recover from the third quarter of 2020, ending five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Private consumption returned to positive growth in the third and fourth quarters, though consumer confidence remained subdued amid the third and fourth waves of local infections and the reimposition of social distancing measures. Buoyed by a brief improvement in business sentiment, overall investment spending also increased in the second half. Partly benefiting from stronger exports of goods, particularly to Mainland China, Hong Kong's goods trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak as global tourism remained at a standstill. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) dragged on GDP in the second half, partly reflecting the slower recovery in exports of goods relative to imports. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021/22 Budget to stimulate the economy, including a one-off HKD 5,000 Consumption Voucher Scheme and a 100% guarantee special personal loan scheme for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, announced in March 2021 an extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, as well as an extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the scheme. These extension measures are expected to help ease cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers.  With COVID-19 vaccines offering the prospect of a return to normal economic activity, Hong Kong's economy is expected to return to positive growth in 2021 as a whole, though the strength and pace of recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, including the development of the pandemic and the pace and efficacy of vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination will take time, the local economy will continue to face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland China economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their large-scale vaccination programmes, which will in turn affect Hong Kong's goods trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts full-year real GDP growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% for 2021, while the average forecast from international institutions and private sector analysts stands at 4.4%.  Labour market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and in early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose further to 7.2% in February 2021, the highest level in 17 years (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, the highest since the SARS epidemic. Total employment stabilised after falling to a low (Chart 3.3), while government figures show that the number of job vacancies continued to decline. The nominal index of payroll per person engaged, which reflects labour earnings, slowed to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. In response to the deteriorating labour market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain staff. Following the conclusion of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support sectors hard-hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labour market is expected to remain under pressure given weak economic conditions. Underlying consumer price inflation declined significantly to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and fell further to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 (Chart 3.4). The three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also remained at a relatively low level, with some slight fluctuations in recent months. Specifically, price pressures on basic foodstuffs eased, and the cost of dining out fell noticeably, reflecting more restaurants offering takeaway discounts during periods of restricted dine-in services. Price pressures on other traded goods (such as durable goods) remained moderate. On the services side, the rental component of the CCPI remained soft as residential rentals consolidated (Chart 3.5).
