Market consensus forecasts for overall headline inflation in 2021 stand at a modest 1.4%, while the Government forecasts underlying inflation of 1% and headline inflation of 1.6% for 2021.  As the COVID-19 pandemic took hold, inbound tourism collapsed rapidly, raising concerns about potential scarring effects on the future recovery of the labour market. This feature therefore empirically examines the impact of a boom in inbound tourism on Hong Kong's labour market, in order to shed light on the potential implications of the current tourism downturn.  Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced significant boom-and-bust cycles (Chart B2.1). Specifically, visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) epidemic in 2003. Following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year, visitor numbers began to surge. Under the original IVS, Mainland China residents could apply to visit Hong Kong on an individual basis once or twice a year, with each visit not exceeding seven days. The IVS was expanded in April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry Individual Visit endorsements to Hong Kong. Visitor arrivals from Mainland China increased substantially thereafter. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure linking Hong Kong with Mainland China, visitor arrivals reached record highs in late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social unrest caused visitor numbers to halve in the second half of 2019, and inbound tourism has been at a virtual standstill since late January 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic.  Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies  We use the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as a case study to examine the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and earnings. We consider the IVS introduced in 2003 as akin to a random economic shock, as it was quasi-exogenous in timing and could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong residents. Our main data source is the demographic data from the Hong Kong population census or by-census. Specifically, we use 5% samples from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011 and 2016 population censuses or by-censuses. In addition, we define tourism-related industries as the catering, retail, hotel and transport sectors.  First, we employ a difference-in-differences analytical framework to compare employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers (aged 20–40) in the treatment group and older workers (aged 41–65) in the comparison group. We assign younger cohorts to the treatment group because they are still at an early stage of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth in inbound tourism. As the impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS on the labour market may change over time, we also employ an event study approach to identify time-varying effects.  Our empirical results show that, compared with older cohorts, younger workers (particularly women and those with only secondary education) were more likely to enter tourism-related industries after the implementation of the IVS. Notably, the effect of the IVS on the probability of young women working in tourism-related industries was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at close to 5 percentage points from 2006 onwards (in terms of the average difference in entry probability relative to the older cohort) (Chart B2.2). We also use a similar method to compare earnings between workers in tourism-related industries (treatment group) and those in non-tourism-related industries (comparison group). The estimation results show that, following the implementation of the IVS, labour earnings growth for workers in tourism-related industries was higher than for employees in non-tourism-related industries. Furthermore, compared with similar employees in other industries, female workers and lower-educated workers in tourism-related industries experienced higher and rising earnings growth (3–20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3).  Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on earnings of female and lower-educated workers  These findings are broadly consistent with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, particularly for young people, women and workers with lower levels of education. In the context of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analyses, namely that robust growth in inbound tourism increased demand for lower-skilled workers and improved the resilience of the lower-skilled segment of the labour market. As inbound tourism moves from boom to bust, these groups of workers may be disproportionately affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to trade close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (CU) level, with the strong-side CUs triggered multiple times during September to October 2020. Strong demand for Hong Kong dollars was mainly driven by equity-related fund demand, including that from buoyant IPO activities and southbound fund inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the aggregate balance increased to over HK$450 billion, HIBORs declined across the board. While uncertainties related to COVID-19 developments, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing US-China tensions might amplify fund flow volatility, Hong Kong's ample foreign reserves and resilient banking system are well-positioned to withstand pressures from such volatility. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate trading close to the strong-side CU level was mainly driven by equity-related fund demand, including that from buoyant IPO activities and southbound fund inflows via the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some IPO proceeds were remitted out, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate remained in a narrow range between 7.7505 and 7.7544 in November and December, supported by improved market sentiment in the local equity market and expectations of higher seasonal fund demand towards year-end. As fundraising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate closed at 7.7568 against the US dollar on 26 February 2021. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the strong-side CUs were triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the aggregate balance, reflecting substantial fund inflows into Hong Kong dollars. From September to October 2020, the strong-side CUs were triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the LERS, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, causing the aggregate balance to increase from HK$193.1 billion at end-August to HK$457.5 billion at end-February (Chart 4.3). The strong-side CUs were triggered a total of 85 times throughout 2020, with cumulative inflows of HK$383.5 billion. From a cross-border perspective, the increase in total deposits showed no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-resident direct investments continued to flow into Hong Kong in Q4 2020, with no indication of any abnormal fund flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised at HKEX Chart 4.3 Aggregate balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index broadly tracked the softening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had limited impact on the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index, the movement of the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked that of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Looking ahead, uncertainties related to COVID-19 developments, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing US-China tensions may amplify fund flow volatility. As an international financial centre, various fundraising activities, such as IPOs, are conducted in Hong Kong, resulting in substantial fund flows into and out of the city. On one hand, such fundraising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, funds raised by listed corporates may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business purposes. Hong Kong's ample foreign reserves and sound banking system are well-positioned to withstand fund flow volatility without compromising financial stability. With continuous fund inflows into Hong Kong dollars, the monetary environment in Hong Kong remained accommodative during the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since end-June 2020, the HKD Monetary Base increased by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). By components, the increase in the monetary base during this period reflected the rise in the aggregate balance resulting from multiple triggerings of the strong-side CUs. Meanwhile, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, government-issued notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the monetary base During the review period, large-scale IPO activities led to increases in Hong Kong dollar deposits arising from IPO subscription loans, causing Hong Kong dollar broad money (HKD M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component to rise significantly during July to October 2020 and January 2021 (Chart 4.6). As IPO activities concluded and customers repaid IPO subscription loans, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels by end-2020. Entering January 2021, HKD M3 increased significantly again, mainly driven by large-scale IPO activities at end-January. Overall, HKD M3 grew by 21.7% over the seven months since end-June, and by a more moderate 9.1% if the effects of the end-January IPO activities are excluded. Based on counterpart asset analysis, excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth of HKD M3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the monetary base triggered by the strong-side CUs (Chart 4.7). As the major component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% over the same period, or by a more moderate 9.1% excluding the effects of the end-January IPO activities. Although HKD time deposits recorded a decline due to low deposit rates, this was more than offset by rapid growth in demand and savings deposits driven partly by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with AIs by currency Chart 4.7 Changes in HKD M3 and counterpart assets Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% over the seven months since end-June. USD deposits fell marginally by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% over the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in renminbi deposits. Overall, due to short-term fluctuations in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO activities, total deposits with AIs rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the end-January IPO activities, total deposits grew by a more moderate 6.4%. It should be noted that monthly monetary statistics may be volatile due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand as well as business and investment-related activities, and should therefore be interpreted with caution. As the aggregate balance increased, HIBORs remained at extremely low levels overall during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite large-scale IPO activities in the second half of 2020, HKD interbank interest rates did not experience significant volatility due to ample liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD interbank interest rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly tracked the movement of the US dollar yield curve, steepening during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared with end-June, the 3-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at end-February, while the 10-year Hong Kong Government Bond yield rose by 67 basis points over the same period to 1.30%. Chart 4.9 Government Bond yields, composite interest rate and average lending rate of new mortgages At the retail level, HKD interest rates largely followed the decline in HKD interbank interest rates. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds of retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at end-June to 0.23% at end-February 2021 (Chart 4.9). As funding cost declined, the average lending rate of new mortgages also fell from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the movement of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the LERS, HKD interest rates are influenced by their USD counterparts. Given the prolonged low interest rate environment in the US, HKD interest rates are expected to remain low, with occasional fluctuations due to capital markets activities and seasonal liquidity demand. Amid a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, ample liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffers to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Both the offshore renminbi (CNH) and onshore renminbi (CNY) exchange rates against the US dollar strengthened since end-May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the relatively better economic outlook of Mainland China compared with the rest of the world, as well as the weakness of the US dollar. FTSE Russell's announcement in late September to include Mainland China government bonds in the World Government Bond Index provided further support to renminbi strength driven by investment demand. For most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium over the CNY exchange rate, averaging around 100 pips in Q4, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and offshore renminbi exchange rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief bouts of volatility due to occasional northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, it remained below 4% for most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month CNH HIBOR followed onshore renminbi rates lower in late December, before rising again in late January, partly due to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-month CNH HIBOR fixings The CNH liquidity pool in Hong Kong continued to grow during the second half of 2020. Since Q4, the pace of renminbi deposit growth accelerated, partly reflecting renminbi appreciation and the relatively higher interest rates of renminbi compared with other currencies. Relative to end-June 2020, the combined outstanding balance of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit grew at a faster pace, reaching RMB826.3 billion at end-January 2021, an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among these, RMB customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by strong growth in deposits from corporate customers. On the other hand, the outstanding balance of certificates of deposit decreased by 25.0% over the same period. Chart 4.12 RMB deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong As for other renminbi business, outstanding renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB159.2 billion over the seven months since end-June 2020. Meanwhile, RMB trade settlements in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven months from July 2020 to January 2021, transactions processed by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,769.5 billion, representing an increase of 16.7% compared with the same period of the previous year. Among these transactions, the increase in remittances from Hong Kong to Mainland China was higher than that of remittances from Mainland China to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong's sizeable CNH liquidity pool is sufficient to continue supporting a large volume of renminbi payments and financial transactions. In 2020 as a whole, the average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system reached RMB1,191.5 billion, compared with RMB1,133.9 billion in 2019.

With economic recession persisting due to the recurring COVID-19 pandemic and the prolonged low interest rate environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined further in the second half of 2020, while asset quality deteriorated slightly. Nonetheless, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient, supported by strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the HKMA decided to extend a number of relief measures to continue supporting the economy through the difficult times. Looking ahead, while the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes for the global pandemic coming under control and the resumption of economic activities, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. Such uncertainties, together with ongoing geopolitical tensions, could weigh on business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic may impair the repayment ability of businesses and households, banks should remain vigilant about the impact of relevant downside risks on their asset quality.  In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, return on assets declined to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared with 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), causing a decline in net interest income that more than offset the modest increase in non-interest income, resulting in lower profitability. For the full year of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%.  Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks  Largely driven by substantial capital inflows into equity markets, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more ample. HIBORs softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. In particular, the three-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points during the second half of the year to 0.35% at end-2020 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The composite interest rate, an indicator measuring the average cost of HKD funds of retail banks, followed a broadly similar trend, falling significantly from 0.71% at end-June 2020 to 0.28% at end-2020 (the green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the composite interest rate mainly reflected falling interbank funding costs and reductions in time deposit rates by some major retail banks.  Chart 5.3 Interest rates  Taking a broader view, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of locally incorporated licensed banks fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (the red line in Chart 5.4).  Chart 5.4 HKD and USD funding costs and maturities of licensed banks  Looking ahead, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging as the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' net interest margin performance. Moreover, despite the breakthroughs in vaccine development that have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain, given the considerable uncertainties surrounding vaccine distribution and efficacy. These risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term.  The capitalisation of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions stood at 20.7% at end-December 2020, well above the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7% during the period, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions was maintained at a healthy level of 8.2% at end-December 2020, well above the statutory minimum of 3% (Chart 5.6).  Chart 5.5 Capitalisation of locally incorporated authorized institutions Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions  The liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period, as measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio requirement under Basel III. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum of 25%.  Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio  The most recent figures under the Net Stable Funding Ratio requirements also indicate stable funding conditions for authorized institutions. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions were maintained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their respective statutory minimums of 100% and 75%. The ample liquidity and stable funding conditions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks.  Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio  Customer deposits remained the primary source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting the maintenance of a stable funding structure in the banking system. At end-2020, the proportion of customer deposits to total liabilities of all authorized institutions hovered at 56.1%, broadly in line with the level six months earlier (Chart 5.9).  Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions  As total deposits of all authorized institutions increased in the second half of 2020, while total lending fell during the same period, the average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions in all currencies declined from 76.0% at end-June 2020 to 72.3% at end-2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, as at end-2020, the average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio and the foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively, compared with 86.4% and 65.5% six months earlier.  Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions  The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Under a shock of a 200 basis point rise in Hong Kong dollar interest rates and their USD counterparts, the potential decline in the economic value of the interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks was estimated to be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at end-December 2020 (Chart 5.11).  Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks  Against the backdrop of recurring pandemic and tightening social distancing measures causing sustained economic recession, total loans and advances declined moderately in the second half of 2020. However, for the full year of 2020, total credit in the banking sector still recorded positive loan growth, though the pace slowed significantly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all authorized institutions, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, contracted by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total lending was attributable to falls in both domestic loans (including loans used in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans used outside Hong Kong. Specifically, domestic loans fell modestly by 0.9% in the second half, while loans used outside Hong Kong contracted by 3.9%, compared with increases of 2.6% and 4.2% respectively in the preceding six months.  Chart 5.12 Loan growth  Analysed by currency, Hong Kong dollar loans, after declining by 2.0% in the first half, were broadly maintained at a level similar to that at end-June 2020 by end-2020. Foreign currency loans, after surging by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, fell by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a moderation in US dollar loan demand as global liquidity conditions improved.  The banking sector's outlook for short-term credit demand was slightly more optimistic than six months ago. The HKMA's Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook for December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed authorized institutions expecting loan demand to increase in the following three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting loan demand to decline during the same period fell to 13% (Table 5.A).  As the pandemic has adversely affected the repayment ability of households and businesses, the loan quality of banks deteriorated slightly, but remained sound by historical and international standards. Moreover, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also moderated in the second half of 2020. The gross CLR of all authorized institutions rose moderately from 0.79% six months earlier to 0.9% at end-2020, while the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans of all authorized institutions increased from 0.49% at end-June 2020 to 0.57% at end-2020. For retail banks, the gross CLR and the ratio of overdue and rescheduled loans rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, global economic performance was sluggish, but inflationary pressures continued to intensify across the world, particularly in the United States. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale pandemic outbreaks, and the possibility that monetary policy tightening could exceed expectations if US inflation proves more persistent and broad-based than anticipated. Should the Federal Reserve tighten monetary policy aggressively and cause global financing conditions to tighten, this would exert pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine could have significant impacts on the global economy through trade and financial channels, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. For the whole of 2021, the growth of total bank loans accelerated. On the other hand, the residential property market has softened since mid-2021. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may threaten the sustained economic recovery, and the possibility of a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of these risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios. The global economy began to slow in late 2021, with weakness extending into 2022, as the highly contagious Omicron variant led to increased mobility restrictions worldwide, while persistent supply bottlenecks continued to weigh on production. Meanwhile, global inflationary pressures continued to intensify amid supply-demand imbalances and labour shortages, and have spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly the United States. More recently, with the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine, the surge in commodity prices could further exacerbate the threat of global inflation, while heightened financial market volatility could lead to an undesirable tightening of global financing conditions, further complicating the global monetary policy outlook. Looking ahead, there is significant uncertainty surrounding the global economic outlook. In the near term, large-scale pandemic outbreaks cannot be ruled out, along with the reimposition of lockdown measures and a renewed deterioration in supply bottlenecks. In the United States, as the risks of inflation being more persistent and broad-based than expected have grown, the Federal Reserve has turned hawkish, accelerating the timeline for tapering asset purchases and raising interest rates, and has begun discussions on reducing its balance sheet. If the Federal Reserve needs to tighten monetary policy significantly, global financing conditions could also tighten, leading to a deterioration in borrowers' debt repayment abilities, and disorderly capital outflows would exert pressure on the recovery of relatively vulnerable emerging market economies. The Russia-Ukraine conflict may pose sustained upside risks to global commodity prices, exacerbate shortages in industrial goods supply, and increase financial market volatility. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Feature 1 examines whether swing pricing — a tool for managing their liquidity in open-ended funds — can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool. In Emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, although the momentum was temporarily dampened as some Southeast Asian economies reimposed stringent pandemic containment measures in the third quarter, while tech-exporting economies in the region (South Korea and Singapore) continued to benefit from robust global demand for technology products. While a broad-based recovery in Emerging Asia is widely expected in 2022, the near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, new variants remain a concern, particularly for economies in the region with lower vaccination rate and limited public health resources. Second, the faster pace of policy normalisation by the Federal Reserve could trigger capital outflows and intensify currency depreciation pressures in the region; economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policies to support their recovery will face a more difficult trade-off between stemming capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. Third, a slowdown in major economies, coupled with a potential shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens, will weigh on the trade growth outlook. Fourth, the rise in prices of various commodities triggered by the Russia-Ukraine conflict will feed through to inflation in the region while simultaneously undermining consumption. With increased global economic uncertainty, the decisions of regional central banks regarding monetary policy normalisation will become more complex. Central banks in economies with weaker growth momentum and inflation that is more sensitive to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs. In the long run, to rebuild sustainable and resilient growth models, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature 2 examines the sensitivity of equity returns to changes in climate risk and how such sensitivity is influenced by firms' environmental performance. Mainland China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by renewed waves of COVID-19 outbreaks, power restriction measures, and tightening measures in the housing market. Looking ahead, with the continued weakness in the housing market and the outbreak of the Omicron variant, the Mainland economy may continue to face downward pressures in the near term. As a result, the Mainland authorities have made stabilising growth their top priority this year and have introduced a series of fiscal and monetary support measures. The total amount of onshore bond defaults and defaults by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) on onshore bonds both declined in the second half of 2021; Feature 3 examines whether the pricing of SOE bonds has improved in recent years. Overall risks in the banking sector remain manageable, as Mainland banks (particularly systemically important banks) have limited exposure to developer loans, low non-performing loan (NPL) ratios, and high provision coverage ratio. Hong Kong's economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, but at a slower pace than in the first half. Seasonally adjusted real GDP grew moderately, as goods exports and private consumption benefited from the continued global economic recovery, improved local labour market conditions, and the government's consumption voucher scheme. On a year-on-year basis, GDP growth was 5.1% in the second half of 2021, compared with 7.8% in the first half. For the whole of 2021, GDP growth was 6.4%, representing the first full-year positive growth since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local pandemic outbreaks and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures have weighed on local economic activity. The government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022-23 Budget to support the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Personal Special Relief Guarantee Loan and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme have been enhanced, with higher maximum loan amounts, extended application periods, and extended repayment periods. The HKMA, together with the banking sector, also extended the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to the end of October 2022. The scheme also provides borrowers with a one-year partial principal repayment option, which also applies to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. Hong Kong's economy is expected to continue recovering on an annual basis in 2022, but at a slower pace than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global growth amid the ongoing pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's goods exports will continue to benefit from the global economic expansion. The government's promotion of various capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support for the economy. The government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% for 2022, while the average growth forecast by international organisations and private sector analysts is 1.6%. However, the strength and pace of economic recovery will be affected by various uncertainties and risks discussed in previous sections, particularly the pandemic and the pace of US monetary policy normalisation. With the economic recovery, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate declining to 3.9% by year-end. Total employment rebounded but remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data showed that labour market pressures re-emerged amid a new wave of local pandemic outbreaks. In addition, a decline in the number of online recruitment advertisements also reflected a reduction in new job vacancies. The new wave of local pandemic outbreaks and the tightening of anti-pandemic measures will exert some pressure on the local labour market (particularly sectors involving face-to-face contact) in the near term. Looking further ahead, labour market conditions will depend on the development of the local pandemic situation and the pace of local economic recovery. Local inflationary pressures broadly increased in recent months but remained moderate. On a year-on-year basis, underlying consumer price inflation edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022. The three-month annualised rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months, partly due to higher prices for dining out and energy-related items. Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to rise slightly in the near term as import prices increase and the pandemic disrupts logistics. However, weak rental prices and moderate local labour cost pressures should help contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts project headline inflation at 2.4% for 2022, while the government projects headline inflation at 2.1% and underlying inflation at 2.0% for 2022. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market. Although the Hong Kong dollar staged a slight rebound in October 2021, the upward momentum subsequently faded, mainly due to weak net southbound capital flows through Stock Connect and market expectations that the US dollar would strengthen as the Federal Reserve normalises monetary policy. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar remained on the strong side of the CUs for most of the time, with trading continuing to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Trading in Hong Kong's interbank market continued to be smooth and orderly. Owing to ample interbank liquidity, HIBORs remained low during the review period. The average lending rate on new mortgage loans rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. The Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Offshore CNH banking business continued to flourish. In particular, Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool continued to expand, with RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit growing to RMB 1,113.5 billion as at end-January 2022. Although outstanding renminbi loans declined, RMB trade settlements in Hong Kong continued to grow. The average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system rose to RMB 1,522.6 billion in 2021. Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore CNH business is expected to benefit from the continued liberalisation of the Mainland capital account, increased demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiatives, supported by Hong Kong's efficient financial infrastructure and the two-way Stock Connect, Bond Connect, and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect schemes. Buoyed by government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, global economic recovery and robust firms' earnings drove major global equity markets to broadly continue rising in the last quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to reach a record high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022. However, growing market concerns about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid sharply rising inflation risks, surging commodity prices, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict have led to consolidation in major global equity markets since early January 2022.

The rapid global spread of virus variants (Delta and Omicron), combined with persistent production bottlenecks, caused a notable slowdown in the global economy in the latter part of 2021, with growth drivers remaining weak as 2022 began. Global inflationary pressures continued to intensify and had spread to a broad range of goods and services in major advanced economies, particularly in the United States. Rising inflation concerns prompted a hawkish shift in the Federal Reserve's monetary policy stance, heightening the risk that a premature tightening of global financing conditions could weigh on currently elevated asset valuation levels, and proving unfavourable for emerging market economies where recovery remained broadly lagged. More recently, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine pushed up commodity prices and triggered financial market volatility, exacerbating some of the aforementioned risks. In emerging Asia, despite the spread of the Delta variant within the region, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, with major technology-product exporting economies in the region continuing to outperform their peers. While the Omicron variant does not appear to have severely disrupted the region's economic recovery, any uncertainty associated with new variants will continue to cast a shadow over the region's economic outlook. In addition, the normalisation of Federal Reserve monetary policy could trigger adjustments in regional asset prices, and a slowdown in major economies could drag on the region's exports of goods growth. The conflict between Russia and Ukraine, on one hand, has driven up commodity prices and increased inflationary risks, and on the other hand, could weaken consumption and increase global economic uncertainty, making the decisions of regional central banks on monetary policy normalisation more complex. Mainland China's economic growth slowed in the second half of 2021, affected by a new wave of COVID-19 outbreaks, power restrictions, and tightening measures in the housing market. Looking ahead, the domestic economy may continue to face downward pressures from a cooling housing market and outbreaks of the Omicron variant. In light of this, the government has designated stabilising growth as the top priority for this year, with macroeconomic policy set to provide greater support.  The global economic recovery slowed markedly in the final quarter of 2021, as the highly transmissible Omicron variant overlapped with the spread of the Delta variant, triggering a new wave of infections and leading to tighter restrictions on movement worldwide. Furthermore, supply chain issues — such as shipping bottlenecks and shortages of key production inputs such as semiconductors — continued to constrain production. Entering 2022, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecast in January that global GDP growth would slow from 5.9% in 2021 to 4.4% in 2022, reflecting the continued drag from the pandemic and supply constraints, reduced policy support in the United States and other major advanced economies, and a slowdown in Mainland China's growth drivers that offset the expected growth rebound in the rest of Asia (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 International Monetary Fund real GDP growth forecasts  As the global economy slowed, inflationary pressures continued to build during the review period. Core inflation (excluding food and energy prices) rose significantly in major advanced economies, particularly in the United States, which had implemented larger-scale policy stimulus since the pandemic. Amid supply chain bottlenecks, pent-up demand being released, and labour shortages, inflationary pressures spread to a broad range of goods and services (Chart 2.2). In addition, the recent military conflict between Russia and Ukraine has pushed up commodity prices of various commodities, which could further exacerbate already elevated global inflationary pressures. Chart 2.2 Core CPI inflation rates for selected economies (1) The latest data for the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Euro area are for January 2022; all others are for December 2021. (2) "Asian advanced economies" includes Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, and Singapore. (3) "Asian emerging market economies" includes Mainland China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Thailand.  Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, with substantial downside risks, and will depend on the evolution of the pandemic and related supply chain disruptions, how geopolitical tensions affect global trade, inflation, and financial market sentiment, as well as the policy response of major central banks to inflation. On the pandemic front, most governments have so far adopted targeted measures in response to the recent surge in Omicron cases, focusing on restricting high-risk activities, encouraging remote working, and promoting vaccination. Compared with previous lockdown policies, these less restrictive measures should help reduce supply chain disruptions, and there have already been early signs of improvement since late 2021 (Chart 2.3). However, should large-scale outbreaks occur, the reimposition of lockdowns cannot be ruled out, which could lead to a renewed deterioration in supply bottlenecks. Chart 2.3 Purchasing Managers' Index – Suppliers' Delivery Times sub-index  If the pandemic remains under control, supply bottlenecks are expected to gradually ease, providing some relief to goods inflation. However, several developments could make the current period of elevated global inflation more persistent than expected, including: the risk that the Russia-Ukraine military conflict and sanctions on energy imports from Russia will push up commodity prices; the risk that rising production costs will be reflected in final selling prices with a lag; the possibility that earlier sharp rises in global residential property prices could drive future rent increases; upside risk to wage growth from tight labour markets; and rising inflation expectations. In particular, given that US inflation has recorded its largest increase in decades, the Federal Reserve shifted to a more hawkish policy stance at its December 2021 Federal Open Markets Committee meeting, no longer characterising high inflation as "transitory," and doubling the pace of asset purchase tapering from USD 15 billion per month to USD 30 billion per month, with a view to ending the asset purchase programme by March 2022, and began discussing balance sheet runoff. Indeed, recent market pricing suggests the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates multiple times in 2022. By contrast, given the Euro area's closer trade and financial ties with Russia and Ukraine, the ECB may face more significant policy trade-offs. Against this backdrop, and given that global debt levels and asset valuation remain elevated amid prolonged policy easing, if persistent inflationary pressures compel the Federal Reserve to tighten policy faster than expected, this could worsen the debt repayment abilities of borrowers and trigger financial market volatility. More recently, as geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe have escalated, risk aversion in financial markets has risen, and signs of US dollar shortages have emerged, including a widening of cross-currency basis swap spreads. Under conditions of premature tightening of global financing conditions, emerging market economies with weaker fundamentals that remain affected by the pandemic could become vulnerable to renewed growth slowdowns, currency depreciation, and capital outflow pressures. Heightened market volatility could also trigger redemption pressures on open-ended funds, increasing their liquidity risks. Feature 1 discusses whether swing pricing — a liquidity management tool for open-ended funds — can reduce the liquidity risks of these funds during periods of market stress, and discusses the potential limitations of this tool.  In emerging Asia, economic recovery continued in the second half of 2021, though the spread of the Delta variant dampened growth drivers in the third quarter, particularly in some Southeast Asian economies (Chart 2.4). Meanwhile, South Korea and Singapore, as major technology-product exporters in the region, continued to benefit from robust global demand for technology products, which further widened the uneven recovery across the region. In addition, inflationary pressures in many emerging Asia economies remained moderate. Chart 2.4 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index  There is broad market expectation for a widespread recovery in Asian emerging market economies in 2022, but the region's near-term economic outlook faces multiple headwinds. First, although the Omicron variant has spread within the region since late 2021, its economic impact has been less severe than that of previous waves of infection; however, economies in the region with lower vaccination rate and more constrained public health resources will continue to face the threat of new variants. Second, the normalisation of Federal Reserve monetary policy could trigger capital outflows and exert currency depreciation pressures on regional currencies. Regional economies that still need to maintain accommodative monetary policy to support their economic recovery will face more difficult trade-offs between curbing capital outflow pressures and supporting economic activity. At the long end of the yield curve, given their historically high correlation (Chart 2.5), the risk of a sudden spike in US long-term yields could spill over into long-term bond yields in emerging Asia, heightening the risk of asset market corrections in the region. Chart 2.5 Correlation between Asian ten-year sovereign bond yields and corresponding US Central Government bond yields  Third, the region's merchandise trade outlook faces uncertainties from slowdowns in major economies and the possible shift in demand from goods to services as the global economy gradually reopens — factors that could weigh on the region's export growth. Chart 2.6 United States: imports from emerging Asia and real GDP  Fourth, while the trade and financial links between economies in the region and Russia and Ukraine are relatively limited, the conflict-induced rise in commodity prices will feed through to regional inflation and simultaneously weaken consumption. Coupled with increased global economic uncertainty, the decisions of regional central banks on monetary policy normalisation will become more complex. Central banks in regional economies with weaker growth momentum and greater sensitivity of inflation to energy prices will face particularly difficult trade-offs.  The pandemic has also reminded regional economies of the long-term need to rebuild more sustainable and resilient growth models to prepare for other risks such as climate risk. To this end, investors need to place greater emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors in their investment considerations. Feature 2 examines whether returns in equity markets are affected by changes in climate risk, and how such sensitivity is influenced by corporate environmental performance.  The COVID-19 pandemic dealt a severe shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turbulence, some open-ended funds experienced large capital outflows (Chart B1.1), placing pressure on their ability to manage their liquidity. Chart B1.1 Capital outflows from selected open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode  Apart from investors' liquidity needs, another possible reason for the large-scale outflows was that investors acted on first-mover advantage by redeeming early, thereby avoiding potentially surging redemption costs under stressed market conditions. To curb capital outflows caused by first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds employ swing pricing — a pricing rule for open-ended funds that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, no empirical research has established whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds.  In this context, this Feature conducts empirical research to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce capital outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby reducing their liquidity risks. In addition, this Feature seeks to identify factors that may have limited the effectiveness of swing pricing during periods of market stress. Based on these assessments, we offer policy recommendations relating to financial stability.  First-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby transferring redemption costs to them. First-mover advantage is primarily present in open-ended funds that use traditional pricing rules, under which the subscription and redemption costs borne by investors in the fund (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund's price after the transaction is executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not have to bear these transaction costs, which creates an incentive for them to redeem early — particularly when large redemption costs are anticipated. Consequently, during periods of market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced as expected redemption costs rise. This amplifies the redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by open-ended funds.

With continued growth in exports of goods and private consumption, the Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021, returning to positive full-year growth for the first time since 2019. Entering 2022, a new wave of local infections and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activity. The economy as a whole is expected to sustain its recovery on a full-year basis in 2022, though the strength and pace will be affected by uncertainties and risks including the pandemic situation and the normalisation of US monetary policy. These headwinds may also affect the labour market outlook following significant improvement in 2021. While local inflation may edge up slightly in the near term amid rising import prices, weak local rents and labour costs should help contain overall price pressures.  The Hong Kong economy continued to recover in the second half of 2021. In year-on-year terms, real GDP grew further by 5.5% in the third quarter and by 4.8% in the fourth quarter (Table 3.A), though the pace of growth moderated compared with the first half. For 2021 as a whole, real GDP grew by 6.4%, marking the first positive full-year growth since 2019.  **Figure 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components**  Quarter-on-quarter, economic activity grew modestly by 0.6% and 0.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively (Figure 3.1). On the domestic front, improved labour market conditions, together with the government's Consumption Voucher Scheme, boosted private consumption. However, aggregate investment spending, after two consecutive quarters of strong rebound, pulled back in the final quarter. Externally, Hong Kong's goods trade performance remained robust amid the continued recovery of the global economy, while trade in services stayed weak, partly because inbound tourism remained at a standstill (Figure 3.2). In net terms, external trade was a drag on GDP growth in the third quarter but provided support in the fourth quarter.  **Figure 3.2 Export and import volume**  A new wave of local infections and the consequent tightening of social distancing measures put pressure on local economic activity in early 2022. The Government launched the fifth and sixth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund, and introduced additional counter-cyclical measures under the 2022–23 Budget to shore up the economy. To support cash flow, the 100% Guarantee Personal Loan Scheme and various guarantee products under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme were enhanced, with maximum loan amounts raised and application and repayment periods extended. The HKMA and the banking sector also extended the "Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme" to end-October 2022. The scheme also offered borrowers a one-year partial principal repayment option, which was likewise applicable to loans under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.  The Hong Kong economy is expected to continue its recovery on a full-year basis in 2022, though the pace of growth will be slower than in 2021, partly reflecting the slowdown in global economic growth amid the persistent pandemic and a higher base effect. Specifically, Hong Kong's exports of goods will continue to benefit from global economic expansion. The Government's push for major capital works and infrastructure projects will also provide support for the economy. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 2.0% and 3.5% in 2022, while the average growth forecast from international organisations and private-sector analysts stands at 1.6%. Nevertheless, the strength and pace of Hong Kong's economic recovery are subject to the many uncertainties and risks discussed in the preceding chapters. In particular, recent pandemic developments, the accelerated pace of normalisation of US monetary policy, and heightened geopolitical concerns (such as the Russia-Ukraine situation) have cast a shadow over the near-term economic outlook for Hong Kong and the world. On the other hand, an earlier-than-expected resumption of quarantine-free travel between Hong Kong and Mainland China could provide an additional boost to local economic growth.  As the economy recovered, the labour market improved further in the second half of 2021, with the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate falling to 3.9% at year-end (Figure 3.3). Total employment in December 2021 also rebounded by 2.0% from its recent trough in February 2021, though it remained below pre-pandemic levels. In early 2022, official data indicated that labour market stress re-emerged amid a new wave of local infections. In addition, a decline in online job advertisements pointed to a reduction in new job vacancies. Looking ahead, the new wave of local infections and the tightening of COVID-19 restrictions will exert some pressure on the local labour market in the near term, particularly in sectors involving face-to-face contact. Over a longer horizon, labour market conditions will depend on the course of the local pandemic and the pace of the local economic recovery.  **Figure 3.3 Labour market conditions**  Local inflationary pressures have broadly increased in recent months but remained moderate. In year-on-year terms, the underlying consumer price inflation rate edged up to 1.1% and 1.2% in the third and fourth quarters of 2021 respectively, and remained at 1.2% in January 2022 (Figure 3.4). The three-month-on-three-month annualised underlying inflation rate, which reflects inflation momentum, also picked up in recent months. Specifically, prices of dining out and some energy-related items rose at a faster pace amid the recovery of local demand and rising external prices (Figure 3.5). Meanwhile, the housing rental component of the CCPI continued to broadly decline, thereby containing overall inflation momentum (Figure 3.6). Real unit labour costs remained subdued but edged up slightly in recent quarters, partly due to some improvement in real average wages (Figure 3.7).  **Figure 3.4 Different indicators of consumer price inflation** **Figure 3.5 Hong Kong import prices** **Figure 3.6 CCPI rental component and market rentals** **Figure 3.7 Unit labour costs**  Looking ahead, local inflation is expected to edge up slightly in the near term amid rising import prices and pandemic-related disruptions to logistics. However, weak rents and mild local labour cost pressures should help contain overall price pressures. Market consensus forecasts put the headline inflation rate for 2022 at 2.4%, while the Government forecasts headline inflation of 2.1% and underlying inflation of 2.0% for 2022.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened during the period under review amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over US monetary policy normalisation. With ample liquidity in the Hong Kong dollar market, HIBORs remained low. Overall, Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money market transactions continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. Looking ahead, while uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund flow volatility, Hong Kong's ample foreign reserves and robust banking system are well-positioned to withstand such volatility. Overall, the Hong Kong dollar traded mostly on the strong side of the CUs, with transactions continuing in a smooth and orderly manner. Since September 2021, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually softened against the US dollar amid risk-off sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the Hong Kong dollar staged a mild rebound in October 2021 as market sentiment improved, the rally subsequently lost momentum, mainly due to weak net southbound flows through the Stock Connect (Chart 4.2) and market expectations of a stronger US dollar as the Fed's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the period under review, IPO-related activities continued to provide support to the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the period under review, with no significant signs of capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, with no signs of abnormal cross-border capital flows. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Net southbound flows through the Stock Connect Chart 4.3 Equity funds raised at HKEX Despite the strengthening of the US dollar during the period under review, the Hong Kong dollar nominal effective exchange rate index remained stable as the renminbi appreciated against the Hong Kong dollar (Chart 4.4). Given the small inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the Hong Kong dollar real effective exchange rate index broadly tracked the movement of the nominal effective exchange rate index. Chart 4.4 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, pandemic developments and escalating geopolitical tensions may heighten fund flow volatility. As US dollar interest rates rise, under the normal operation of the LERS, outflows of HKD funds (the pace and scale of which will depend on market conditions at the time) could potentially lead to a weakening of the Hong Kong dollar and trigger the weak-side CU. Hong Kong also possesses ample foreign reserves and a sound banking system capable of withstanding fund flow volatility without compromising financial stability. During the period under review, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative. The HKD Monetary Base rose 1.4% over the eight months since end-June 2021, driven mainly by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting continued issuance to meet sustained demand from banks for Exchange Fund Bills under ample banking system liquidity conditions, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes increased by HK$119.7 billion to HK$1,188.7 billion during the period under review, with the Aggregate Balance (before discount window operations) declining correspondingly by HK$119.9 billion to HK$337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued notes and coins remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes Total deposits of authorised institutions grew moderately by 4.5% in the six months since end-July 2021, while Hong Kong dollar deposits edged up by 0.3%. It should be noted, however, that monetary statistics may be subject to volatility due to various short-term factors, such as seasonal and IPO-related funding needs and business and investment-related activities, so it is more appropriate to look at longer-term trends. For the whole of 2021, total deposits and Hong Kong dollar deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Chart 4.6 Deposits of authorised institutions by currency Overall, Hong Kong's interbank market continued to operate in a smooth and orderly manner. Thanks to ample liquidity in the banking system, HIBORs remained at low levels despite market concerns about monetary policy tightening in the US (Chart 4.7). HIBORs edged up slightly in December 2021, partly reflecting market expectations of higher funding demand towards year-end. The average lending rate for new mortgage loans rose slightly from 1.48% in July 2021 to 1.56% in January 2022. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the period under review, ranging from 5.00% to 5.50%. Looking ahead, ample liquidity in the banking system will provide a sufficient buffer during major capital market activities or periods of financial market volatility. Chart 4.7 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar HIBORs During the period under review, the offshore renminbi interbank market continued to function normally. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards year-end, the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced mild volatility in late December 2021, while the three-month CNH HIBOR remained relatively stable, hovering around 3% throughout the period under review (Chart 4.8). Chart 4.8 Overnight and three-month CNH HIBOR fixings In the second half of 2021, Hong Kong's CNH liquidity pool continued to grow steadily. In the six months since end-July 2021, RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit outstanding increased by 30.3%, reaching RMB1,113.5 billion at end-January 2022 (Chart 4.9 and Table 4.A). Among these, RMB customer deposits increased by 33.5%, driven mainly by corporate fund inflows, offsetting a 48.0% decline in certificates of deposit outstanding. Chart 4.9 RMB deposits and certificates of deposit in Hong Kong In the six months since end-July 2021, while outstanding renminbi loans declined by 10.2% to RMB167.6 billion, RMB trade settlements in Hong Kong continued to grow. During the period from end-July 2021 to end-January 2022, transactions processed by banks in Hong Kong amounted to RMB3,763.0 billion (Chart 4.10), an increase of 18.3% compared with RMB3,181.0 billion in the same period last year. Hong Kong's large CNH liquidity pool continued to support a significant volume of renminbi payment and financing transactions. For the whole of 2021, the average daily turnover of the RMB RTGS system increased from RMB1,191.5 billion in 2020 to RMB1,522.6 billion. Chart 4.10 RMB trade settlement remittances Looking ahead, Hong Kong's offshore CNH business is expected to benefit from the establishment of two-way Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect, Bond Connect and Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect, the continued opening up of the Mainland's capital account, growing demand from international investors for renminbi assets, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area development. Major global equity markets continued to rally in Q4 2021, but consolidated from January 2022 onwards amid growing market concerns about tightening stances of major central banks in advanced economies and escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. The local stock market remained subdued in Q4 2021, dragged down mainly by a sharp decline in technology stocks. Global risks and uncertainties surrounding Hong Kong's pandemic situation caused the Hang Seng Index to fall to a near two-year low at end-February. Meanwhile, the CNH debt market in Hong Kong continued to grow steadily in the second half of 2021. The residential property market has softened since mid-2021, partly affected by weakened asset market sentiment and a new wave of the pandemic locally. Major global equity markets broadly continued to rise in the final quarter of 2021, leading the MSCI World Index to reach an all-time high of 3,262 points on 4 January 2022 (Chart 4.11). Supported by global economic recovery and strong firms' earnings amid government monetary and fiscal policy stimulus, major global equity markets maintained their upward trend, though the pandemic remained investors' key risk concern throughout the year. However, major global equity markets consolidated from early January 2022, as markets grew increasingly concerned about the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies amid a sharp rise in inflation risks, surging commodity prices and the escalating Russia-Ukraine conflict. By contrast, at end-2021, Hong Kong's equity market continued to lag behind other major global markets. The Hang Seng Index hovered between 24,000 and 26,500 points from September to mid-November, closing at 23,398 points at end-2021, a decline of 14.1% from 2020. At the beginning of 2022, the return of buying interest from value investors to the local stock market pushed the Hang Seng Index back up to around 25,000 points in January. However, uncertainties surrounding Hong Kong's pandemic situation and the intensifying Russia-Ukraine conflict dragged the Hang Seng Index to a near two-year low of 22,713 points at end-February. Over the entire period under review from end-August 2021 to end-February 2022, the Hang Seng Index fell by 12.2%, while the MSCI World Index declined by 5.2% (Chart 4.11). Chart 4.11 Hang Seng Index and MSCI World Index Due to the emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant, option-implied volatilities in equity markets surged sharply in late November 2021 before subsequently easing. Although the SKEW Index retreated from its historical high in late June 2021, it remained elevated, reflecting investors' willingness to pay more for downside protection against a correction in the prolonged equity market rally since the onset of the pandemic (Chart 4.12). Chart 4.12 Option-implied volatilities of the Hang Seng Index and S&P 500, and the SKEW Index Against a backdrop of ample global liquidity, Hong Kong equities continued to record net inflows from international investors since the last report (Chart 4.13). In contrast, the southbound leg of the Stock Connect recorded significant net outflows in Q3 2021, mainly due to concerns about the impact of Mainland regulatory changes on technology stocks. However, southbound buying through the Stock Connect began to recover in December 2021, recording cumulative inflows of HK$98.3 billion through end-February. During the period under review, cumulative net buying increased by 5.7% to HK$2,233.0 billion (Chart 4.14). For the whole of 2021, there were 98 new IPO listings, raising a total of HK$328.9 billion (Chart 4.15), a decrease of 17.8% in total funds raised compared with the previous year. In 2021, HKEX ranked fourth globally in the IPO market, behind only NASDAQ, the New York Stock Exchange and the Shanghai Stock Exchange. Chart 4.15 Hong Kong IPO market The outlook for the local stock market remains uncertain. The easing of Mainland monetary policy and more Chinese concept stocks seeking secondary listings in the primary equity market in Hong Kong would improve market sentiment in Hong Kong's equity market. However, the equity market continues to face a number of headwinds, including uncertainties surrounding the local pandemic situation, a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalisation, and the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Profitability of Hong Kong retail banks declined in the second half of 2021. The classified loan ratio edged up slightly in the second half of 2021, but remained low by historical and international standards. The Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient against a backdrop of strong capital and liquidity positions. During the review period, the HKMA extended a number of support measures to further assist the economy through difficult times. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant could pose a threat to economic recovery, while the risk of faster-than-expected normalisation of US monetary policy would pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolio.  In the second half of 2021, overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 16.1% compared with the same period in 2020. The weak profitability was mainly attributable to lower net interest and non-interest income, as well as higher operating expenses. As a result, return on assets fell to 0.50% in the second half of 2021, compared with 0.61% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.1). For the full year of 2021, overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks decreased by 18.6% compared with 2020, while return on assets fell from 0.77% to 0.59%. Specifically, the three-month HIBORs edged up by 9 basis points from six months earlier to 0.26% at end-December 2021 (the blue line in Chart 5.3). The funding costs of retail banks remained stable during the review period. In particular, the composite interest rate, which measures the average cost of HKD funds of retail banks, rose modestly by 3 basis points from 0.18% six months earlier to 0.21% at end-2021 (the green line in Chart 5.3). While normalisation of US monetary policy may signal improvement in banks' profitability, near-term improvement could be partially offset by two factors. First, although the Fed signalled multiple rate hikes in 2022, past experience has shown that local rate movements could lag behind US interest rate movements (particularly when liquidity in the Hong Kong interbank market remains very ample). Therefore, improvement in banks' net interest margins may take more time to materialise. In addition, a surge in Omicron variant cases could also introduce uncertainties to the pace of economic recovery, thereby putting pressure on banks' asset quality and profitability. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions was recorded at a solid level of 7.9% at end-2021, exceeding the statutory minimum of 3%.
