Climate change affects every aspect of our lives, and everyone has a responsibility to play their part in mitigating its impact. In this regard, the HKMA has invested considerable efforts in advancing Hong Kong's climate goals and contributing to enhancing global climate resilience and sustainable development. Following last year's inclusion of our first sustainability report as a chapter in the HKMA's 2021 Annual Report, this year we have published the 2022 Sustainability Report as a standalone document for the first time. I hope this report will give readers a deeper understanding of the HKMA's strategies and priorities in strengthening the Hong Kong banking system's capacity to address climate change, building a green finance ecosystem, and fulfilling our role as a responsible investor and sustainable institution. During the year, we made significant progress in advancing sustainability work across the HKMA's major functions. Readers will find details of our specific measures and work in this report, with the following key highlights:  Banks face climate risk in their day-to-day operations. As a banking regulator, the HKMA has taken concrete steps to strengthen banks' capacity to respond to climate change. In 2022, we formulated a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the supervisory process and explored how technology can help banks assess the impact of physical risks. In view of the growing number of green and sustainable products offered by banks, we also shared with the industry good practices on how to properly manage such products, with a view to enhancing banks' climate risk management capabilities.  The HKMA actively participates in various collaborative initiatives on addressing climate risks and promoting sustainable finance. Locally, we are working with other financial regulators through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group) to develop a local green taxonomy framework, which will enhance transparency in the financial markets and bring greater consistency to green finance policies. At the international level, we are actively engaging with a number of international organisations to help formulate policies on addressing climate change and assess its impact on financial stability.  Hong Kong is well-positioned to meet Asia's demand for green and sustainable financing. Despite 2022 being a challenging year for the global bond market, green and sustainable debt issuance in Hong Kong continued to record strong growth of 42%, with total issuance rising to US$80.5 billion, making Hong Kong the largest hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bond issuances². The relevant issuers included the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government and the People's Government of Hainan Province, whose issuances once again demonstrated Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating the flow of green and sustainable capital between the Mainland and international markets.  The flourishing of Hong Kong's green bonds market is partly attributable to the Government Green Bond Programme. Since 2019, the HKMA has helped the Government issue nearly US$16 billion worth of green bonds in total, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, energy efficiency and conservation. We also helped the Government achieve two "firsts": in May 2022, we assisted the Government in issuing the first tranche of Government Green Retail Bonds totalling HKD20 billion, which was at the time the world's largest green Retail Bonds issuance. We also helped the Government issue its first tokenised green bond in February 2023. This was the world's first tranche of tokenised green bond issued by a government, and the issuance marked a milestone in our successful combination of strengths in the bond market, green and sustainable finance, and fintech.  Standards, data and talent are essential elements for the healthy development of a climate finance ecosystem, and require the efforts and collaboration of different sectors to build. To this end, the HKMA works primarily through the Steering Group with other relevant government departments, regulators, academic institutions and the financial industry to develop these elements. In addition to the aforementioned work on developing a local green taxonomy framework, the Steering Group has also promoted skills training in the industry and improved Hong Kong's data resources through its Green and Sustainable Finance Centre. Furthermore, the Steering Group has made good progress in other areas such as mandatory disclosure of climate-related information and carbon market opportunities.  In 2022, the HKMA further strengthened the Exchange Fund's responsible investment work, in particular by setting a target to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions for the Exchange Fund's portfolio by 2050. We also enhanced our risk management work to improve the Exchange Fund's climate resilience and risk-adjusted long-term returns. In addition, to fully capture the opportunities that climate change may bring, we are committed to promoting sustainable investment in the Exchange Fund, seeking investment opportunities that support climate transition and climate change mitigation to enhance the portfolio's long-term returns. By end-2021, the weighted average carbon intensity of the Exchange Fund's equity portfolio had fallen by 43% compared with the 2017 level. Indeed, the Exchange Fund's exposure to high-carbon assets has consistently been lower than that of the overall market. Going forward, we will continue our journey towards net-zero emissions by continuously strengthening the integration of environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into our investment management process, actively exercising asset ownership, maintaining ongoing engagement with stakeholders, and focusing on decarbonisation and transition in the portfolio.  At the HKMA, the Corporate Social Responsibility and Sustainability Committee, which I chair, is responsible for formulating the HKMA's sustainability strategy. Our strategic direction is built on three pillars: environment, staff and social responsibility. On the environment front, we are committed to promoting a green working environment and advocating for a more environmentally friendly market for the public. On the staff front, as a responsible and caring employer, we actively foster a healthy and inclusive working environment. On the social responsibility front, we are dedicated to improving the public's financial literacy, promoting financial inclusion, and giving back to the community.  Compared with the levels when we began tracking our carbon footprint in 2015, we achieved double-digit reductions in per capita greenhouse gas emissions, energy consumption and paper usage in 2022. More importantly, we have developed a roadmap to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier. In the near term, our goal is to fully eliminate Scope 1 emissions and reduce Scope 2 emissions by 63% by 2030 or earlier, using 2015 as the baseline.  Addressing climate change and promoting sustainable development require sustained efforts and collaboration from multiple parties. On this important global issue, we understand the need to lead by example and work together with like-minded peers and international organisations. In the next section, we will outline the HKMA's near-term plans and priorities in addressing climate change across its major functions. Achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 or earlier is a formidable task, and we will spare no effort in pursuing this goal. We are confident that with the collective efforts of all our colleagues, the financial industry and the general public, we will be able to successfully meet the climate challenges ahead.  Eddie Yue Chief Executive

In 2023, the HKMA will continue to drive sustainable development in Hong Kong's financial industry and fulfil its responsibilities as a responsible investor and sustainable institution. At the same time, through participation in international and regional organisations, the HKMA will strive to promote the broad development and best practices of green and sustainable finance. As a regulator of the banking sector, we will work to strengthen the climate resilience of the banking sector and further improve our green finance ecosystem to support banks' green transition. Specifically, the HKMA will engage with banks to understand their progress in implementing climate risk management supervisory requirements, incorporate climate factors into our supervisory review process, and revise the banking sector's "Green Baseline" common assessment framework. The HKMA will also support banks in enhancing their climate resilience and risk management capabilities, for example, by exploring various measures and technological solutions to help banks identify, measure and monitor their climate risk exposures. The HKMA will also collaborate with banks to conduct the next round of climate risk stress-tested exercises as part of the 2023–2024 supervisor-led regular stress-tested process. Participating banks will be required to assess their ability to withstand climate risk under an enhanced stress-tested framework covering multiple stress scenarios, including extreme weather events and adverse economic conditions. To promote the healthy development of green and sustainable investment products offered by banks, the HKMA will keep abreast of local and international market and regulatory developments, maintain communication with the industry, and provide guidance on the sales process in a timely manner. We will also conduct off-site thematic reviews to gain a comprehensive understanding of the green and sustainable investment products offered by banks. In the meantime, to strengthen the green finance ecosystem in support of the financial industry's green transition, the HKMA is planning to consult the industry on the structure and key elements of a local green classification framework. In terms of market development, to promote Hong Kong as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA will assist the Government in scaling up the issuance of green bonds under the Government Green Bond Programme and broadening its scope to cover sustainability bonds, while attracting more green financing activities to Hong Kong through the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme. The HKMA will also assist in implementing the Government-funded Green and Sustainable Finance Training Pilot Scheme to expand Hong Kong's talent pool in green finance. Furthermore, the HKMA will continue to encourage more Mainland local governments, institutions and enterprises to conduct green financing through Hong Kong, and explore the feasibility of integrating green finance with technology. On another front, we will continue to collaborate with other government agencies through the Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group on cross-sectoral topics such as skills training and data, green taxonomy, climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. Through the Green Commercial Banking Alliance, the HKMA will jointly launch various dedicated programmes with the International Finance Corporation in Asia, including conducting green finance research, providing unique market analyses, offering targeted professional training for banks, and providing practical guidance to help banks develop roadmaps for growing green finance as a core business. Looking ahead, the Green Commercial Banking Alliance will work closely with its cornerstone members, global partners and knowledge partners to launch a membership programme to expand the Alliance's influence across Asia. The Green Commercial Banking Alliance will also strengthen the professional capabilities of industry practitioners, facilitate the sharing of green finance knowledge, and lead new initiatives in emerging areas. As a responsible investor, the HKMA has set a target to achieve net-zero emissions for the Exchange Fund portfolio by 2050 or earlier, as part of its commitment to engaging in global climate action and implementing the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures. Looking ahead, the HKMA will continue to incorporate environmental, social and governance factors into its investment management process, work towards the goal of net-zero emissions, and fully support global climate action efforts. As a responsible and sustainable institution, the HKMA cares for both its staff and the wider community and environment. We have developed a sustainability roadmap and set climate targets for our own operations as part of our commitment to global decarbonisation and climate action efforts. The HKMA will continue to prioritise carbon reduction and encourage staff to give their full support in saving energy and reducing waste. In addition, we will provide further guidance to staff on incorporating sustainability principles into procurement processes. To achieve digital transformation and enhance operational agility, the HKMA will explore ways to modernise internal systems and applications to further improve work efficiency while minimising the potential risks that may arise during the digital transformation process.

Climate change is a major risk facing the financial system. The HKMA has been committed to strengthening Hong Kong's financial system to build a greener and more sustainable future, contributing to Hong Kong's climate goals and the global sustainable development agenda. Banks are exposed to a wide range of sustainability and climate-related issues in their day-to-day operations. To continue to fulfil their important role in the financial system and to channel more funds towards green and sustainable projects, banks must proactively manage climate risk. As the banking regulator, the HKMA places particular emphasis on building banks' capacity to respond to and manage climate risk, and on accelerating banks' efforts to support the transition to a low-carbon economy. The HKMA also supports banks in enhancing their capability to detect environmental crimes, and participated in the recently published Hong Kong Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment, which covers areas such as environmental crimes and illegal wildlife trafficking. In 2022, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (Basel Committee)¹ published principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks and responded to frequently asked questions, clarifying how the existing Basel framework addresses such risks. In response to these international developments, the HKMA will continue to work towards integrating climate-related factors into the supervisory framework. Following the issuance of Supervisory Policy Manual module GS-1 "Climate Risk Management" in 2021, the HKMA has maintained dialogue with banks to exchange views on expectations, progress and challenges in implementing the relevant supervisory requirements. To further strengthen the supervision of banks' climate risk management, the HKMA has developed a two-year plan to incorporate climate risk factors into the bank supervisory process, which was communicated to the banking sector in June. As part of the implementation of the two-year plan, the HKMA issued a revised Supervisory Policy Manual module SA-1 "Risk-based Supervisory Framework" and enhanced the CAMEL² rating system by integrating climate risk into the risk-based supervisory process. In the meantime, drawing on lessons learned from the 2021 pilot exercise, the HKMA has refined the climate risk stress-tested scenarios and assessment framework. The HKMA has also made plans to incorporate the next round of climate risk stress tests into the regulator-led regular stress tests, to enable a more comprehensive assessment of the banking sector's resilience under extreme climate scenarios. Under the two-year plan, the HKMA is also enhancing its green assessment framework for banks to reflect the latest developments in sustainability-related issues, including climate risk management and transition planning. At the same time, the HKMA is reviewing the supervisory review process used to assess and monitor banks' capital adequacy levels and determine their Pillar 2 capital requirements, with the aim of encouraging banks to strengthen their risk management frameworks to address risks related to climate change and the transition to carbon neutrality. Given the growing prevalence of banks issuing green and sustainable products, the HKMA conducted a thematic review focusing primarily on how banks develop and continuously manage these products. The HKMA identified a number of good practices during the thematic review and issued a circular in December to share these with the industry, facilitating banks in progressively strengthening their climate risk management capabilities. The application of technology can improve data availability and enhance banks' capacity to manage climate risk. The HKMA has begun developing a common platform for banks to assess the impact of physical risks on real estate. In addition, the HKMA, together with other central banks and regulators, completed a project under the BIS Innovation Hub to explore how technological solutions can facilitate physical risk assessments. The HKMA also attaches great importance to promoting sustainable and globally leading anti-money laundering practices, employing advanced analytics and regtech, complemented by fully automated regulatory data collection. Over the past 12 months, the HKMA has streamlined the anti-money laundering regulatory data collection process to reduce the manual burden and paper usage for banks. To enhance transparency across financial markets and align green finance policies more closely, the HKMA has worked with other financial regulators to establish a local green classification framework. Green classification frameworks, commonly referred to as green taxonomies, classify economic activities as green or sustainable, providing a reference for authorities and market participants to determine whether an activity or its related products are genuinely green or sustainable. To this end, the HKMA has engaged with the industry and other relevant stakeholders to explore the features and challenges of such a framework in depth, and is preparing to make proposals and conduct a consultation on the structure and core elements of the framework in the first half of 2023. Recognising the potential financial risks that climate change may pose to the financial system, the HKMA has incorporated a broader range of climate factors and scenarios into its financial risk analysis and research to enhance current surveillance efforts. The HKMA takes climate change into account in its ongoing monitoring of financial stability risks and incorporates analysis of climate-related risks in its various financial stability reports. Through active participation in the scenario design and analysis workstream under the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), the HKMA has helped to further enrich the climate scenarios to enable central banks and regulators to better understand the macroeconomic and financial impacts of climate change. On the research front, the HKMA conducted a number of applied research projects in 2022 to explore two key topics: greenwashing in corporate green bond markets³ and the role of disclosure in mitigating climate risk exposure⁴. The findings of these studies contribute to the development of policy and regulatory measures to address the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Locally, the research helps to strengthen the HKMA's ongoing monitoring and assessment of the impact of climate risk on financial stability. Externally, the HKMA has shared the research findings with a wide range of stakeholders through various channels, including international central bank research conferences and the HKMA's Half-Yearly Monetary and Financial Stability Report. The HKMA's liquidity facilities framework is a secured standby funding arrangement that provides timely liquidity support to banks in need. The HKMA is studying the incorporation of sustainability considerations when assessing eligible collateral under this framework. The HKMA actively participates in international and regional discussions on addressing climate risk and mainstreaming sustainable finance. Through such participation, the HKMA helps to foster international and regional policy dialogue on addressing climate change and its implications for financial stability, and draws insights to help strengthen the climate resilience of Hong Kong's financial system.

To consolidate Hong Kong's position as a regional green and sustainable finance hub, the HKMA has stepped up efforts to enhance market awareness and participation, provide necessary infrastructure and enablers, and support international initiatives to align with global standards. The Cross-Agency Steering Group on Green and Sustainable Finance (Steering Group), co-led by the HKMA and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), is responsible for coordinating the financial sector's response to climate and environmental risks, accelerating the development of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong, and supporting the Government's climate strategies¹. The Steering Group's work is guided primarily by its strategic plan, which sets out six priority areas and five action themes to strengthen Hong Kong's financial ecosystem and build a greener and more sustainable future (Figure 1). These include: strengthening climate-related financial risk management to reinforce Hong Kong's position as a global risk management centre; promoting the flow of climate-related information across all levels to facilitate risk management, capital allocation and investor protection; enhancing the skills of industry practitioners and raising public awareness and understanding; encouraging product innovation and research measures to direct fund flows towards green and sustainable projects; capturing opportunities arising from the Mainland to develop Hong Kong as the green finance centre of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA); and strengthening regional and international cooperation.  Actions taken to advance sustainable finance development in Hong Kong to date: The Steering Group has made good progress since its establishment. Current priorities include skills training and data collection under the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance (see below), green taxonomy (see "Establishing a Green Taxonomy Framework to Facilitate Green Fund Flows" in the chapter "Building a Sustainable Financial System" on page 9), climate-related disclosures and sustainability reporting, and carbon market opportunities. In particular, the Steering Group published in March a preliminary feasibility assessment of Hong Kong's carbon market opportunities and will support Hong Kong's development as a regional carbon trading centre, including the development of an international high-quality voluntary carbon market and the capturing of opportunities arising from GBA cooperation. In December, the Steering Group announced a collaboration with CDP² to enhance data availability and strengthen sustainability reporting in Hong Kong. As part of this collaboration, both parties developed a climate and environmental risk questionnaire targeting non-listed companies and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), facilitating companies in conducting sustainability reporting and assisting financial institutions in collecting and analysing company-level data for risk assessment and related business decisions. This marks an important step in the Steering Group's efforts to expand the scope of its data work to include SMEs, an important but previously less accessible segment of the economy.  The Steering Group established the Centre for Green and Sustainable Finance in July 2021 to coordinate training and policy work among financial regulators, government departments, industry stakeholders and academic institutions, and to build a resources and data repository. In the first half of 2022, the Centre launched three repositories covering data, training information and internship opportunities respectively, helping the financial sector and other industries access data and learning resources related to green and sustainable finance. The resource repository provides data sources for assessing Hong Kong's physical risks. To support talent development in the industry, the Centre assisted the Government in December to launch the "Green and Sustainable Finance Pilot Training Programme", which provides subsidies for practitioners, students and graduates participating in green and sustainable finance-related training and upskilling. Other measures to promote skills training include the launch of a "Sustainable Finance Internship Programme" to create more internship opportunities for students, and the development of a new "Green and Sustainable Finance" module under the HKMA's "Banking Professional Development Programme"³ for banking practitioners.  "Green and Sustainable Finance Pilot Training Programme"  The HKMA has also been actively supporting the development of green and sustainable finance in the region. In November 2020, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the HKMA launched the "Green Commercial Banking Alliance"⁴, bringing together regional financial institutions, banking industry organisations, research institutions and technology providers to develop a collaborative platform for green commercial banking. The Alliance aims to enable commercial banks and other financial institutions to realise their full potential in developing green finance as a mainstream core business and to promote the engagement of the financial system in global climate change-related activities. The Alliance operates as a one-stop mutual learning platform for financial institutions to access the knowledge, tools and information needed to develop their own green finance roadmaps and transform into credible green financial institutions; convenes green finance leaders and facilitates communication among green financial institutions across different emerging markets while exploring frontier topics; and advances the global green finance agenda to unlock boundless green and climate-related investment opportunities.  In June, five leading global financial institutions⁵ became cornerstone members of the Alliance, working closely with the IFC and the HKMA to encourage clients to adopt green strategies, promote best practices for green products and services, and unlock new business opportunities to facilitate the green economic transition. In addition, three global partners and one knowledge partner⁶ committed in 2022 to providing climate expertise in areas ranging from innovation and standardisation to academic research. Details of the Alliance and its membership structure are available on the relevant webpage (English version): Cornerstone Members, IFC and HKMA sign Memorandum of Understanding.  Since March 2021, the Alliance has organised 18 training activities and roundtables, attracting more than 6,000 participants from around the world, including the Asia-Pacific region, Europe, the Middle East, Africa and the Americas. In addition, the Alliance jointly published its first frontier research report with the Hong Kong Monetary and Financial Research Centre⁷ in June 2022, entitled "Climate Risk: Definition, Measurement, Current Practices and Regulation".  The HKMA has continued to promote the issuance of green and sustainable debt and to nurture the local ecosystem for related professional services. The total amount of green and sustainable debt (including bonds and loans) issued in Hong Kong in 2022 reached US$80.5 billion, representing a growth of 42%. +42% Green and sustainable debt issuance (US$80.5 billion)  To demonstrate the Government's commitment to addressing climate change, promote green finance, and pursue the development of Hong Kong as a more sustainable and liveable city, the Government launched the "Government Green Bond Programme" in 2018, with the HKMA assisting in the implementation of relevant green bond issuances. The Government has to date issued nearly US$16 billion equivalent in green institutional and retail green bonds, with the proceeds allocated to more than 40 green government projects, including green buildings, waste management and resource recovery, and energy efficiency and conservation. To enhance transparency and accountability under the programme, the Government publishes an annual Green Bond Report detailing the allocation of green bond proceeds and the expected environmental benefits.  To enable members of the public to participate in Hong Kong's sustainable development through investment and share in its benefits, the first tranche of Green Retail Bonds with a total value of HKD20 billion was issued in May, receiving enthusiastic public support and becoming the world's largest green retail bonds issuance at the time. The issuance also broadened the range of green and sustainable finance products available in Hong Kong, consolidating Hong Kong's position as a leading green and sustainable finance hub both regionally and internationally.  The Government also continued its regular green institutional bond issuance in the 2022-23 financial year, issuing US$5.75 billion equivalent of green bonds in January 2023. The tri-currency issuance covered US dollars, euros and renminbi, with tenors ranging from 2 to 30 years, continuing to provide important benchmarks for potential issuers in Hong Kong and the region. The issuance was well received by the global investment community and successfully attracted new investors who had not previously participated in the Government's green bond issuances, reflecting investors' confidence in Hong Kong's long-term credit standing and economic fundamentals. In response to investor demand, the Government doubled the issuance size of the renminbi bonds to RMB10 billion. The participation of international investors and Mainland investors through the southbound leg of Bond Connect also increased, demonstrating Hong Kong's position as a leading offshore CNH business hub and further consolidating its status as an international financial centre.  The HKMA also assisted the Government in February 2023 to issue a tokenised green bond for institutional investors, to test the use of distributed ledger technology for bond issuance and settlement. This was among the world's first tokenised green bonds issued by a government. The primary issuance was settled on a T+1 basis on a private blockchain network, with subsequent processes (including coupon payments, secondary market transaction settlement and redemption at maturity) also digitalised. The experience gained from this government issuance can serve as a reference for market participants interested in conducting similar bond issuances in the future.  To provide the industry with credible and accessible market information, the HKMA continued to collaborate with the Climate Bonds Initiative and the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) to publish annual reports on Hong Kong's and the region's green debt markets respectively. The ICMA report showed that Hong Kong became the largest hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bonds issuances in 2022, with a total of US$27.8 billion in bonds arranged through Hong Kong, accounting for more than approximately one-third of the regional total. Largest hub in Asia for arranging international green and sustainable bonds: US$27.8 billion.  Following its inaugural issuance in 2021, the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government issued RMB5 billion in offshore local government bonds in Hong Kong in November 2022, including RMB2.6 billion in green and blue bonds⁸. In the same month, the People's Government of Hainan Province also issued for the first time RMB5 billion in offshore bonds in Hong Kong, including blue and sustainable bonds. These bond issuances once again highlighted Hong Kong's unique role in facilitating green and sustainable fund flows between the Mainland and the rest of the world, as well as its enduring status as the region's premier fundraising platform.  The HKMA continued to promote and implement the "Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme" launched in 2021 and utilised it to attract more relevant professional service providers (including financial institutions, green advisory firms and external review providers) to establish and expand their businesses in Hong Kong. The Scheme has been well received by the industry. As of end-2022, the Scheme had covered the pre-issuance, post-issuance or both external review service costs for the issuance of more than 180 green and sustainable debt instruments, helping issuers ensure and demonstrate strict adherence to market best practices and international standards. Starting from March, the Scheme was optimised by lowering the minimum loan threshold for applying for external review fee subsidies from HKD200 million to HKD100 million, facilitating smaller enterprises in accessing green financing.  Following the successful proof-of-concept for tokenised retail green bonds under Project Genesis in 2021, the HKMA and the BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre again collaborated under Genesis 2.0 to explore the technical feasibility of digitalised carbon forwards (also known as Mitigation Outcome Interests, or MOIs), with a view to enhancing the transparency, objectivity and green credentials of the green bond market. The project was completed in October 2022, successfully developing two prototypes that utilise blockchain and other relevant technologies to track, deliver and transfer digitalised MOIs.

As one of the largest asset owners and managers globally, the HKMA plays an important role in promoting green and sustainable finance to support the global climate change agenda. The HKMA is also a pioneer in responsible investment, having led investments in green and sustainable assets as early as 2015, requiring its external investment managers to adopt the Principles of Responsible Ownership published by the Securities and Futures Commission, and integrating environmental, social and governance factors into the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The HKMA invests prudently in accordance with the principle of "preserving capital first, and achieving long-term growth", believing that emphasis on environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors can unlock long-term sustainable value in investments and mitigate associated risks. In the face of increasingly severe climate change challenges, the HKMA continues to advance on its responsible investment journey, including setting a "Net Zero by 2050" target in 2022 and refining risk management strategies to enhance portfolio resilience, thereby seeking better risk-adjusted long-term returns for the Exchange Fund. The HKMA also actively participates in building the green and sustainable finance ecosystem, working with like-minded investors and regulators to promote responsible investment, and collaborating with international organisations to develop ESG investment standards. Transparency of climate-related information plays a pivotal role in managing climate risk. To fulfil its commitment to supporting the Glasgow Declaration published by the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) at the 2021 United Nations Climate Change Conference and to greening the global financial system, the HKMA makes climate-related disclosures for the Exchange Fund in accordance with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) under the Financial Stability Board. a. TCFD — Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures The Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Financial Secretary, sets the responsible investment framework and guiding principles, which are implemented by the Exchange Fund Investment Office in the investment management of the Exchange Fund. The primary guiding principle is to enable the HKMA to prioritise ESG investments with comparable risk-adjusted long-term returns vis-à-vis other investments, in pursuit of the Exchange Fund's investment objectives. Details of the HKMA's responsible investment framework are available on the HKMA website. The Investment Committee under the Exchange Fund Advisory Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, is responsible for overseeing ESG and climate-related risks in Exchange Fund investments. The Investment Committee reviews the responsible investment framework and risk management guidelines, and monitors progress in ESG integration and the ESG status of the Exchange Fund through regular meeting reports from the Risk Management and Monitoring Division of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. As shown in Exhibit 1, the ESG Committee established under the Exchange Fund Investment Office, chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is responsible for coordinating and overseeing various ESG initiatives of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Motions discussed and work progress at each ESG Committee meeting are reported to the Chief Executive Officer of the Exchange Fund Investment Office. Monitoring and governance structure for responsible investment: The dedicated team in the Risk Management and Monitoring Division works closely with the various investment teams of the Exchange Fund Investment Office on ESG integration, and assists the senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office in managing ESG and climate-related risks and opportunities across different types of investments: Public market investments — The Credit, Compliance and Monitoring Committee, comprising senior management of the Exchange Fund Investment Office, monitors the ESG status of the fixed income portfolio through regular reports from the Risk Management and Monitoring Division. In addition, the Risk Management and Monitoring Division participates from an ESG perspective in the selection, appointment and monitoring process of external investment managers for the equity portfolio (see the section "Striving to Exercise Active Ownership" under "Risk Management" on page 27). Private market investments — The Investment Committee, chaired by the Chief Executive of the HKMA, considers ESG-related assessments made by the Risk Management and Monitoring Division and the private market investment team for each investment proposal. Concrete evidence² continues to demonstrate the significant impact of climate change and associated risks. According to the latest report³ of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), even assuming full implementation of the Nationally Determined Contributions announced by various regions, global temperatures are estimated to rise by as much as 2.1 to 2.4 degrees Celsius by 2100, making it difficult to achieve the Paris Agreement's target of limiting the increase in global average temperature to below 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Should regions adopt more aggressive policy measures to close the temperature gap, the resultant transition risks⁴ and asset repricing by markets based on anticipated future trends, compounded by inherent physical risks, would further intensify pressure on asset valuation. In light of updates to global warming trajectories and model assumptions, the HKMA has leveraged the expertise of external consultants to assess the resilience of the Exchange Fund "portfolio" under the "Disorderly Transition" scenario (Exhibit 2), in addition to the scenarios evaluated in 2021. The "Disorderly Transition" scenario incorporates higher transition risk factors over the short, medium and long term, assuming that policy changes and technological developments jointly drive a rapid decline in carbon emissions, while multiple assets are subject to abrupt divestment to keep the average temperature rise below 1.5 degrees Celsius before 2100. This scenario is broadly consistent with the disorderly scenario recommended by NGFS for forward-looking climate impact assessments. The "portfolio" is able to maintain resilience over the medium to long term, given that a larger proportion of its asset allocation is in sovereign bonds, which are less sensitive to the impact of the transition. Sector distribution is key. Low-carbon electricity and renewable energy assets stand to benefit from the relevant transition. Transition risks and asset repricing may adversely affect performance, particularly equity assets, in the short term. The "portfolio" as a whole will be increasingly impacted by physical risks that gradually materialise over time. Energy and conventional utilities remain the most vulnerable sectors. Climate scenarios, like other modelling approaches, have their limitations. The analysis is based on the sector distribution of market benchmarks at the strategic asset allocation level and does not take into account the effects of active security selection within individual sectors. More in-depth research reveals that investments within the "portfolio" are generally more resilient to, or less adversely affected by, transition shocks compared to the market benchmarks of the strategic asset allocation. This further affirms that the HKMA's responsible investment with a focus on combating climate change enhances portfolio resilience. The climate change trajectory remains uncertain, and scenario analysis methodologies will continue to evolve as data quality improves and policies develop. The HKMA will periodically review the relevant scenarios and refine its assessments to better ascertain the Exchange Fund's resilience in the face of climate change. As a long-term investor, the HKMA fully appreciates the risks and opportunities that climate change may present. The HKMA is committed to further expanding sustainable investments and seizing opportunities related to the climate transition, mitigating climate risk and enhancing the portfolio's long-term returns. The HKMA sustained its positive momentum in 2022 by increasing its holdings of green, social and sustainable bonds by a further 50%. On the equity investment front, the HKMA invested in an active equity portfolio with a governance theme, and adopted a decarbonisation strategy favouring companies with lower carbon emissions for its passive equity portfolio. In addition, the HKMA is exploring the establishment of a dedicated private equity portfolio with the dedicated partners of the Exchange Fund's "Long-Term Growth Portfolio" to promote green and sustainable development in Asia (Exhibit 3). Exhibit 3: Continued implementation of measures to increase ESG investments The HKMA has invested in a pan-African wind farm operator that, in addition to generating clean energy, places great emphasis on social and biodiversity factors. Prior to the establishment of the wind farms, local villagers used poison bait to prevent predators from preying on their livestock, which inadvertently endangered certain vulture species classified as endangered. As livestock represents a vital asset for local villagers, the operator constructed livestock shelters within the wind farm to protect livestock from natural predators. In addition, the operator employed a bird monitoring team to issue warnings and shut down wind turbines when vultures were spotted being attracted to animal carcasses occasionally left behind by predators, preventing vultures from being struck by the blades. Reducing predation of livestock created a win-win outcome: on one hand, it safeguarded the livelihoods of local villagers; on the other, it reduced instances of vultures being fatally struck by wind turbines, thereby protecting the endangered species. Good ESG practices can bring more business opportunities and open up revenue streams for companies, as illustrated by the following supply chain-related operations. The investee company is a Mainland China-based integrated logistics and warehousing operator specialising in cold chain pharmaceutical, chemical and high-end consumer goods logistics services. The company faces continuously rising ESG operational standards, driven primarily by multinational corporate customers requiring their service providers to meet high decarbonisation targets aligned with the Paris Agreement. In response to these demands, the company engaged external consultants to help formulate a "Three-Year ESG Plan" to reduce carbon emission intensity by 50% by 2030 or earlier. This comprehensive decarbonisation plan had already delivered significant results in 2021 alone. These ESG initiatives earned the company the "Low-Carbon Green Management Case" award from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing. These achievements and accolades have enabled the company to secure numerous business opportunities from consumer goods and chemical multinational corporate customers that place particular emphasis on ESG practices. The growth of ESG investments is closely linked to the development of the green and sustainable finance ecosystem. The HKMA actively collaborates with like-minded investors and partners to promote responsible investment and enhance industry capabilities. The HKMA successfully hosted the 4th Annual ESG Workshop in 2022, exchanging good ESG practices with 9 participating private market institutions (including dedicated partners, limited partners and corporates) and promoting sustainable investment opportunities in the Asia-Pacific region and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area. On the public markets front, the HKMA encouraged trading partners (mainly investment banks) to expand their ESG headcount and research capabilities, particularly in Hong Kong. At the international level, the HKMA actively participates in the development of industry ESG investment standards and practices: As one of the earliest central bank signatories to the Principles for Responsible Investment (PRI), the HKMA participates in PRI-coordinated collaborative actions among signatories to develop a standardised responsible investment due diligence questionnaire for private equity and venture capital investments⁵,⁶, to assist private market investors in conducting ESG assessments of dedicated partners and investment proposals. The HKMA participates in multiple working groups to support FCLTGlobal's research on key market practices for long-term portfolios and decarbonising private assets, as well as their application to long-term investors. As a member of NGFS and a supporter of TCFD, the HKMA contributed to the NGFS "Climate-Related Financial Disclosures by Central Banks Guidance" to demonstrate the HKMA's commitment to adopting good ESG practices. The HKMA also leads a workstream under the NGFS "Net Zero for Central Banks" working group to participate in formulating sustainable and responsible investment guidelines for the central banking community. The HKMA continues to participate in various industry forums and seminars, sharing insights on responsible investment and climate change strategies.
